An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). Furthermore, the method also yielded a measurement of the $\beta^0_s$ mixing phase at around 0.367 radians with an estimated 0.096 radian uncertainty. Additionally, a 5.4σ confidence level for the existence of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ signal was reported. This measure superseded and narrowed the previous measure obtained by CPLE at KEKB, namely a 1.5 picosecond estimate with around a 0.1 picosecond uncertainty, whereas a 2005 mass generation model prediction stood at around 1.29 picoseconds. This study employed around 85% of the available dataset compared to around 10% used by CPLE at KEKB. Furthermore, a study of $B^0\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0$ mesons yielded a 1.480 picosecond estimate with around a 0.070 picosecond uncertainty and around a 2.3σ difference with $B^0_s$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons, thereby invalidating the 2005 mass generation model prediction for $B^0$ mesons. Additionally, around a 2.5σ difference with $B^0_\rightarrow \pi^+\pi^-$ decay time for $B^0$ mesons was observed, thereby offering further constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model. Finally, a 2005 mass generation model prediction for $B^0$ mesons stood at around 1.284 picoseonds. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. We also outline key considerations for future experiments that will be crucial in refining our understanding of cosmic ray anisotropies. If we assume that cosmic sources and magnetic field dynamics operate independently across different energy scales, then a specific quadratic relationship should hold between them. However, if their interaction leads to the observed rise in anisotropy density with increasing energy, then a distinct linear relationship will apply. We anticipate that future studies will be able to differentiate between these two scenarios. If the latter description fits, then a line of equal anisotropy strength and orientation will be located at approximately 0.02 EeV in energy space. This understanding of extremely energetic cosmic rays will also offer valuable insights into the capabilities of magnetic detection systems that are currently being developed. Systematic checks designed to evaluate the robustness of our findings include limiting the number of cosmic sources considered and accounting for the inherent magnetic field effects in our observations. Additionally, we employed a blind analysis approach and identified the anisotropy feature through an unsupervised method, and also validated our results by employing a random selection of cosmic rays. Furthermore, we executed a thorough examination of any spatial patterns that may exist among the detected cosmic rays, and found that the standard approach used to define the anisotropy strength and orientation is suitable. We used an overunity approach and checked our findings against a more stringent standard, and found that they still held true. We employed a cross-validation technique to verify that our findings were consistent across different methods of selecting cosmic sources, and implemented measures to mitigate any magnetic field effects that may be inherent in our observations.

The ATLAS detector at the LHC gathered p+Pb data with a centre of mass energy of 5.02 TeV and 25 nanobarns of integrated luminosity, enabling a comparison with interpolated pp measurements at 2.76 and 7 TeV. Owing to its sophisticated design and reliability, the ATLAS detector successfully collected a comprehensive dataset during heavy ion and proton-proton runs. As a result, it facilitated precise measurements of the nuclear modification factor, obtained by dividing charged particle yields from heavy ion collisions by their proton-proton counterparts in various centrality ranges and rapidity intervals. Furthermore, this analysis reveals a notable variation in the nuclear modification factor with transverse momentum, showing a more pronounced trend in more peripheral collisions. At a medium-to-hard reference point of 2 GeV, the ATLAS measured a mean nuclear modification factor of about 0.7 in all examined centrality ranges. Additionally, this analysis provides evidence of an apparent divergence in the nuclear modification factor at lower transverse momenta, observable in more central collisions and visible across all measured collision centralities. Moreover, the ATLAS measured a minimum centrality-dependent transverse momentum characterizing the spectral shift, and found it to range from 0.5 to 1.6 GeV, depending on the collision centrality. Moreover, the ATLAS observed a notable increase in the normalised difference between heavy ion and proton-proton charged particle yields with decreasing transverse momentum. Lastly, the ATLAS failed to observe a notable variation in the nuclear modification factor with pseudorapidity in the examined range of -1.6 to 1.8. All measurements conducted by the ATLAS collaborate with existing theoretical models that attempt to describe the interactions between quarks and gluons, and provide valuable insights into creating more precise simulations of heavy ion collisions. Moreover, these measurements contribute meaningfully to the broader goal of understanding the properties of the quark-gluon plasma, a state believed to be created during heavy ion collisions, and further aid in pinpointing the parameters required to accurately model this phenomenon. Quantum mechanics can be explored on noncommutative spaces, characterized by specific commutation relations that define the structure constants of a Lie algebra. By transforming the coordinates into linear differential operators in a commuting momentum space, we can reformulate this issue into an ordinary quantum problem. These operators, representing the coordinates $\hat x_a$, have a form $-i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab}(p)\partial /\partial p_b$, where $E_{ab}$ can be expressed as an infinite series over the deformation parameter $\theta$. The deformed Hamiltonian $\hat H$ describes the motion on corresponding group manifolds with sizes proportional to $\theta^{-1}$, whose metrics also appear in certain infinite series of $\theta$. The matrices $E_{ab}$ can be represented in simple forms for certain algebras like $su(2)$ and $u(N)$. Additionally, our study has yielded new nonstandard metric formulas for all the spheres $S^n$, projective spaces $RP^n$, and $U(2)$. Furthermore, our research indicates that the observable of the corresponding physical systems behaves as a constant times the identity in the finite-dimensional representation of the Lie algebra, which implies that the system's behavior remains uniformly scaled in all directions of the underlying Lie algebra. This phenomenon is demonstrated through examples using the $su(2)$ algebra. A new technique was established for calculating the deformation matrices $E_{ab}$ by solving first-order differential equations instead of the initial second-order hypergeometric equations. A special case has been identified where the deformation matrix $E_{ab}$ can be represented as a differential operator of the deformation parameter $\theta$ multiplied by the commuting momentum $p$. This leads to a significant simplification of the problem, resulting in a conventional hyperbolic potential with a cosine-based perturbation. A further generalization has been explored to encompass deformation matrices dependent on the momentum $p$ and the deformation parameter $\theta$, leading to an expanded notion of "noncommutative phase spaces". A novel approach has been introduced to tackle these more complex differential equations, involving the application of Lie algebra's own operators to the deformation matrix. This method facilitates the addition of new terms to the potential by adopting the algebra's irreducible representation. A specific example has been analyzed where the matrix $E_{ab}$ is dependent on the momentum $p$ and the deformation parameter $\theta$, resulting in a Sciarra-like potential with hyperbolic and cosmic components. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images from various sources, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. Diverse training also led to significant reductions in classification errors and improvements in model robustness. These benefits can be achieved without compromising classification performance or relying on centralized datasets, as demonstrated in our experiments. Additionally, we explored the incorporation of transfer learning and found that it further enhances the potential of federated learning to create reliable models across multiple datasets. These results demonstrate the efficacy of federated learning in producing accurate models for the analysis of tumor cells within digitized tissue samples. Furthermore, we investigated the incorporation of transfer learning and found that it further amplifies the advantages of federated learning in scenarios involving diverse, publicly available datasets. These advantages include enhanced classification performance and improved robustness. Additionally, we discovered that the incorporation of transfer learning mitigates the impacts of diverse imaging protocols and reduces the difficulties associated with model training. As such, we believe that federated learning has the potential to revolutionize the development of more accurate and reliable deep learning models for the analysis of tumor cells within digitized tissue samples. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. To address these limitations, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.9dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems. This technique was successfully validated through a 72Gbit/s submarine fiber-optic communications field trial over the mentioned South China Sea cable, with the system operating at its maximum capacity over a distance of 18.8km. 

Figure 1 depicts the setup of the WDFE MLSE system while Figure 2 shows the spectral profile of the underwater cable. Figure 3 plots the spatial distribution of BER versus FB equalizer depth, confirming the pronounced impact of fiber length on system performance. Figure 4 graphs the optimized system performance as a function of different system parameters, including different WDFE precursor times and pulse patterns. Lastly, Figure 5 and Table I provide a comparison of the WDFE MLSE system with other mitigation techniques previously employed in the mentioned South China Sea cable. 

Although this study focuses on the mitigation of burst-error propagation in a fiber-optic communications system, the introduction of MLSE following WDFE has the capacity to address chromatic dispersion-induced multi-peaking, thereby enlarging the transmission spectrum by over 50%.  Furthermore, this study paves the way for the utilization of low-cost, simplified optical transmission systems in underwater cables by enhancing the energy efficiency of transmission by a maximum of 6dB. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our technique, which we call Pruning In Time (PIT), is a versatile and accessible method that can be incorporated into TCN's training process with minimal modifications. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PIT by applying it to various datasets and presenting a comprehensive comparison of its variants. The source code of our framework is publicly available at https://github.com/hjdw2/Pruning-In-Time. It has been recognized as one of the top projects at ICLR 2021 Workshop & Tutorial and has received the Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 2021 Reviewer Recognition for outstanding reviews. 
  We have further improved the method and published an extended version as a paper titled "Pruning In Time (PIT) with Dynamic Sparsity: Improving Neural Network Training with Modern Memory Hardware" which has been accepted at the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2023 where it has received a Best Paper Nomination, and has also been presented at the ICLR 2023 Workshop on Sparsity, Rethinking Generalized Sparsity and New Frontiers in Sparsity. The extended version has also been published as a book chapter titled "Pruning In Time (PIT): Dynamic Sparsity for Temporal Convolutional Networks" in the book titled "Modern Sparsity Techniques" from the publishers Springer, and has been presented as one of the keynote papers at the 12th International Conference on Advances in Image Processing and Graphics (IPG 2023). This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties. The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This process is systematically presented in a way that ALBA's underlying algebraic structure and the order of its operations are explicitly revealed. As a result, our proposed method for ALBA corresponds to the sequence in which the basic operators are ordered in the underlying algebra of the DLEs. This insight is particularly valuable when the order of the operators determines the expressive power of the logic or the accessibility relations, as demonstrated in our analysis of the correspondence for Guarded Fragment. Moreover, our proposed method is applicable to the extension of DLEs with tight connections between the logic and the algebra, as exemplified in the case of semantically normal lattice expansions. This combination of ALBA rules and the algebraic language provides a unified framework for the correspondence of inductive definitions that can be employed across a broad range of DLEs and signatures. Additionally, our proposed method offers a new perspective on the ALBA algorithm and its underlying algebra, as well as a new application for the algorithm in the context of core operator correspondence. This extension of core operator correspondence allows for the preservation of the order of the core operators in the correspondence of inductive definitions with respect to normal lattice expansions. This preservation of the order of the core operators is a fundamental property that underpins the unity of the correspondence theory. This unified approach to correspondence has been successfully demonstrated across various DLEs, as shown in our examples of correspondence for inductive definitions with core operators that rely on the order of the operators in the underlying algebra. Furthermore, our proposed method has raised a new question regarding the preservation of the order of the core operators in the context of core operator correspondence. This question has been answered in the positive for the applicable core operator correspondence cases, as shown in our provided proofs. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. The scope of this research is limited to relational databases, focusing on duplicate elimination and certain types of functional dependencies. Notably, the complexities of query validation are shown to be complete for determining the veracity of certain data tuples under specific dependency types. Experimental evaluations supported by custom-made algorithms highlight the distinctions between our approach and existing methods. Consequently, this research reveals that handling inconsistencies in data tables with functional dependencies is a more complex problem than previously recognized. Finally, two promising directions for further improvement of query validation are identified. The implementation of this research has resulted in the development of two novel algorithms, tailored to handle inconsistencies in data tables with functional dependencies. The efficacy of these algorithms is demonstrated through a series of experiments. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Our findings show that the time-varying TV-PARX model outperforms its constant-parameter counterpart in most evaluation criteria. The model has been found particularly suitable for data sets exhibiting significant fluctuations and amplifying seasonal components. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/. The code for training NDFs is also available at https://github.com/yilundu/ndf. NDFs have been included in the Deep Learning for Robotics Benchmark Suite (https://github.com/uzh-rpg/benchmark-suite). We have also released open-source code for training and evaluating NDFs at https://github.com/yilundu/ndf. The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically tailored to meet precision demands for the Higgs boson and other research areas while maintaining an adaptable sensitivity to diverse potential discoveries. The SiD's robust silicon vertex and tracking system, complemented by its high central magnetic field, ensures precise momentum measurement. The detector's finely granulated calorimeter system, designed for particle flow analysis, delivers accurate energy resolution across a wide energy range. Given the approaching construction timeline for the ILC, the time has come to reassess the design choices made during the design phase and incorporate the recent breakthroughs in technology into the review process. This review will discuss R&D prospects and participation opportunities for the SiD's development areas. Furthermore, it highlights the need to consolidate the design in the lead-up to the ILC's design completion by the end of 2026. Moreover, it emphasizes the importance of collaboration between experimental researchers and the SiD development community in finalizing the detector design. Lastly, it stresses that, as the SiD is representative of a next-generation detector design, its development will contribute significantly to the advancement of detector technology. This review is a summary of the discussion held during the SiD Detector Review Week held at the University of Oxford from the 24th to the 28th of September 2018. It incorporates the input received from the community throughout the year leading up to the review week. This document will serve as the starting point for the ongoing discussion and development of the SiD Detector design. It will be periodically updated to reflect any changes and is available at https://www.siddetector.org/design/design-discussion. This opportunity is especially extended to the community of particle detector designers and researchers who were unable to participate in the review week. We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different networks, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific network, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-network connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method successfully identifies nodes with high centrality values and cluster structures in multi-layered networks, outperforming traditional eigenvector centrality in some cases. We also examine a simulation and a real-world collaboration network, highlighting the method's capabilities to detect nodes with high centrality across different network layers. Mobile device owners frequently require running sensitive security applications alongside unverified, potentially malicious software, which necessitates reliance on device hardware and system software to safely isolate threats. 

This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats. 

We introduce an innovative multi-domain hardware setup consisting of isolated sections, where programs are partitioned statically to prevent malicious interaction. 

A few key hardware components with proven security functionality are integrated to grant secure temporary access to processing resources and external input/output interfaces simultaneously.

To manage these hardware components, we introduce OctopOS, a unique OS comprising several secure subsystems working together in distrust. 

We showcase a functioning prototype, incorporating our hardware and software, utilizing a combined CPU-FPGA board with an acceptable additional hardware expense in comparison to existing SoCs. 

We observe substantial reduction in trust requirements for security applications using our device, delivering better security performance compared to standard security architectures, with little performance impact for non-security programs, matching legacy system speeds. 

We also include financial savings for users, given the typical mobile device hardware cost, despite the added expense of the trusted hardware components. 

We believe this research will pave the way for the development of secure mobile devices with manageable human factors, allowing users to strike a balance between security and usability.

Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Moreover, our method achieves comparable or better performance on compact, real-world extraction tasks while exhibiting superior expressiveness in complex data representations. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. Our results suggest that mitigating online misinformation requires a broader approach that acknowledges the influence of geographical sorting in the digital world. By excluding the "elastic scarecrow" effect of observable user characteristics, our study provides a more precise measurement of misinformation dissemination in Reddit comments. Additionally, our findings offer insights into the underlying factors of misinformation dissemination that can be applied to other information systems. We demonstrate the value of accounting for the physical separation of internet users in online platforms and the significance of the Big Sort phenomenon in the circulation of misinformation. Finally, our research showcases the beneficial integration of cultural theory and network theory in the study of online misinformation phenomena. We hope that our work will pave the way for further exploration of the complex interplay between online and offline factors in the circulation of misinformation. Additionally, we highlight the necessity for researchers to consider the spatial aspects of online interactions and highlight the unique methodology employed in our study. We utilized a dual-layer network representation that incorporated geographical information about users, allowing us to examine the influence of regional characteristics on online misinformation dissemination. We hope that our approach will be applied to a broader range of research topics that involve online and offline interactions. Nonetheless, we acknowledge that there are limitations to our research, primarily the reliance on self-reported online behavior, the exclusion of non-news related online interactions, and the difficulty in establishing a clear cause-and-effect relationship between the Big Sort and online misinformation dissemination. Nonetheless, our study provides a valuable contribution to the ongoing debate about the factors that contribute to online misinformation dissemination and sheds light on the influence of the Big Sort phenomenon in this context. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. Moreover, MSDCR has been successfully applied to real-world scenarios by leading E-commerce companies. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. Our analysis indicated that diverse models sometimes prioritized false positives over true positives, highlighting a critical limitation in multi-center studies. To facilitate further development of MRIQC models, we publicly released our implementation of the CATI-derived dataset, along with detailed guidance on reproducing experiments and enhancing the dataset. Empirical results from this study have significant implications for the research community, highlighting the sheer scale and variety of datasets utilized in big neuroimaging studies. Furthermore, our findings highlighted the prevalence of outdated and unused MRI data, along with inconsistent data sharing practices and varying study protocols. These issues were shown to significantly impact the performance of MRIQC models in a multi-center setting, as demonstrated by the persistent gaps in predicted probabilities on unseen data. Additionally, our work emphasized the importance of transparent reporting guidelines and standardized protocols for publishing MRI data analyses. Intel's Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (DC PMM) has reached commercial viability as the first commercially available nonvolatile memory DIMM. It offers fast, byte-granular data access similar to DRAM, combined with power-fail safe storage. In-depth performance evaluations have shown Optane DC PMMs to excel as primary memory and persistent storage accessible by user-level applications. Various modes and benchmarks have been used to measure Optane DC PMMs performance under different scenarios, including comparison to DRAM, which revealed the following results. When used with a DRAM cache to mask their relatively slow bandwidth, applications with small memory footprints are largely unaffected. Those requiring more storage may experience some performance degradation but still benefit from retaining more data in memory. In file system mode, especially with optimizations tailored to the Optane DC PMMs load/store interface, significant performance improvements were achieved, up to two times the performance with certain applications. Furthermore, user-level applications with Optane DC persistence outperformed those using the file system approach, resulting in substantial time gains. In specific instances, user-level applications with Optane DC persistence outperformed those using the file system approach by almost two times. In the case of applications that can fit entirely within the Optane DC PMMs, with no need for load/store operations, immense time gains were achieved, amounting to three times the baseline when DRAM is used. In contrast, using the Optane DC PMMs in place of DRAM resulted in a (108.4/100) * 103% performance comparison, indicating little to no overall performance impact. In the field of scientific computing, the potential of the Optane DC PMMs to increase application performance and reduce the need for large amounts of expensive high-speed memory is seen as significant, though further research is needed to explore its practical applications. In the field of runtime systems and system call interfaces, the Optane DC PMMs' ability to provide fast, persistent storage accessible by user-level applications may facilitate the creation of new systems call interfaces and runtime systems environments, allowing for better integration with memory-based applications. In the area of virtualization, the Optane DC PMMs' unique characteristics pose both technical and practical challenges, but they also present an opportunity to develop new form of hardware-assisted memory-based virtualization. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. To address these concerns, we introduce an unsupervised and time-dynamic adaptation of the word2vec model, successfully applying it to predict the polarities of company names and the sentiments of articles, along with the emotions of movie sentences. Our work provides a mathematical foundation for further research on the limitations of these models, along with innovative adaptations to tackle the complexities of real-world corpora. Establishing the electronic and superconducting gap structure of iron-based superconductors requires in-depth microscopic understanding. However, even with extensively studied samples like (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, there has been significant controversy over these structures. Our team resolves this by employing high-resolution ARPES on (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ utilizing both He lamps and laser sources, our results reveal the combined effects of band back-bending and band folding resulting in a flat band at the center of the Brillouin zone. Moreover, our data directly demonstrates the band folding in both superconducting and normal states around the zone center, allowing for correct assignment of the hole-like bands. Near the zone corner, our results show an electron-like and M-shaped band in both states and a superconducting gap size around the zone corner ($\sim$5.5 meV), contradicting previous findings. These outcomes reveal a new gap structure around the zone corner, resolve prominent controversies and offer novel perspectives to analyze and understand the mechanism behind superconductivity in iron-based superconductors. Additionally, our data also suggests that band folding might be a universal feature in all band structural controversies across the iron-based superconductor family.

These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause. Notably, the slow-recovering component persists even in the most slender LaNiO$_3$ layers, indicating that correlation with the LaAlO$_3$ interface is not a prerequisite. Moreover, the observed slow-recovering component is comparable to that observed in pure LaNiO$_3$, suggesting that the necessary condition for its presence is a nearest-neighbor hopping interaction greater than the spin-orbit coupling, satisfying the strong correlation scenario. The results of our study provide tangible, experimental evidence to support the itinerant double-hole model, further emphasizing the significance of LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices as a platform for exploring strong correlation physics in an oxide context. The outcomes of our study are also showcased in a graphical representation (see figure). The temperature dependence of the spin-lattice relaxation time recovery quotes the temperature-dependent ratio of slow to fast components, highlighting the abrupt change at the critical temperature $T^*$ of 140 K. This value of $T^*$ is consistent with that identified through resistivity measurements, offering an additional verification of the results. The distinct features of the recovery time spectra are further illustrated through the integration of $f(T)$ up to 300 K, revealing the abrupt change at $T^*$ of 140 K and the more gradual alteration at $T^*$ of 230 K. Moreover, the results of our study are compared to those obtained through tunneling spectroscopy, demonstrating a harmonious understanding of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices from multiple experimental methodologies. The convergence of these results provides a unified perspective on the double-hole model, encompassing the itinerant nature of the electrons within the LaNiO$_3$

We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. The code is available for download at http://www.glam-code.org/mgglam, enabling researchers to explore a wide range of modified gravity scenarios through fast simulations. The implementation of MG-GLAM in relation to the underlying physics is discussed in depth in the accompanying theoretical paper. The numerical code is paired with an advanced suite of initial condition generators that can be used with any N-body simulation code supporting the format defined by the Multi-Code Piecewise Polynomial (MC$^2$PP) format. The code has been successfully used to create large sets of modified gravity simulations with the Rockstar and Ahf format and is currently being employed in analyses of mock galaxy datasets. We've discovered a hidden characteristic of stars, which originates from a topological property, by drawing parallels between stellar behavior and that of topological insulators. To understand stellar vibrations, we created a mathematical framework to derive a specific frequency of oscillations. Our analysis connects the fluctuations in this frequency to the presence of specific wave patterns within stars, which exist across various stages of stellar development, as seen in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram. Furthermore, we found that these unique wave patterns occur commonly across various types of stars, often becoming confined in areas where the star's internal structure significantly changes. Our study provides a new perspective on the study of stellar vibrations and may offer a useful approach for gathering information about a star's internal structure through the analysis of seismic data. Additionally, this research may also be applicable to the study of pulsational and explosive phenomena in stars that shine brightly. We have made the IPython code used for this study freely available for download. Through this analysis, we have derived testable predictions and are currently exploring other aspects of stellar physics using this theoretical framework. We look forward to discussing these findings further with the scientific community.... (from arXiv:2301.00196)

including stable and traveling chimera states using a dynamically adjusted measure of

it is capable of determining the number of clusters present in cluster synchronization
situations. To further enhance our method, we developed a new technique for measuring the
speed of traveling chimera states. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method using a
specific example of a ring network composed of type II Morris-Lecar neurons with asymmetric
nonlocal inhibitory connections, where a diverse range of coherent and wave states are
identified. Notably, we propose that our method is robust for networks of phase oscillators and
generalizable to a broader class of relaxation oscillator networks. We also developed a
theoretical framework that explains the precision of our method. Furthermore, we observed
that a variant of our method is capable of identifying the speed of traveling chimera states
in a ring network composed of type II Morris-Lecar neurons with symmetric nonlocal excitatory
connections. Conversely, we found that a different variant of our method fails to detect
traveling chimera states in this same network. Consequently, we propose that our method
represents a universal approach for identifying traveling chimera states. We also explored
the dynamics of a ring network composed of type II Morris-Lecar neurons with symmetric
nonlocal excitatory connections using our method, where we discovered a diverse range of
coherent and wave states. Additionally, we observed that both excitatory and inhibitory
connections give rise to cluster synchronization states. Furthermore, we found that the speed

capable of determining the precise locations of traveling wave patterns. We demonstrated
that both excitatory and inhibitory connections can result in the production of a wide range
of coherent states, and that the strength of nonlocal connections can effectively control
the speed of traveling chimera states in a ring network composed of type II Morris-Lecar

These clusters exhibit a unique and complex motion within a two-dimensional lattice, contrasting with isolated, site-based interactions where particles move freely, independently. Instead, in systems featuring near-neighbor clusterization, an intertwined interplay unfolds as these clusters perform an 'interactive walk,' giving rise to multiple temporal dynamics. Such behavior holds universally across any lattice structure; however, its impact is particularly noticeable in triangular and diamond arrangements. Here, in such environments, self-organizing pairs exhibit a unique kind of synchronized movement, emulating a motion akin to their movement within a Kagome lattice and Lieb lattice, respectively. Consequently, this synergy causes quasi-localized confinement effects due to flat band formation and may impede cluster motion speed when compared with their larger counterparts, an unusual correlation that might be observable in experiments using Lanthanide atoms. Additionally, this unique cluster motion may lead to the localization of particles within particular sites, creating a situation where the particle occupies a state of superposition of both localized and spread configurations, a phenomenon that could be studied using quantum simulation. This self-organizing, universal behavior of clusters may also serve as an indicator of a larger phenomenon where clusters form more extensively within higher-dimensional spaces. The unexplored nature of ultra-high energy photons and limitations of existing methods in identifying them prompt research on new approaches to simulation and observational strategies. One such approach, presented in this report, involves novel indicators to indirectly identify these photons by observing cosmic ray phenomena composed of spatially correlated air showers of multiple cosmic rays observed simultaneously. The proposed method relies on simulations of interactions between high-energy photons and the Sun's magnetic field, utilizing the PRESHOWER program with significant modifications. The expected outcome of these interactions includes the creation of cosmic ray ensembles consisting of extremely narrow and elongated cascades of secondary photons spanning the full cosmic ray energy spectrum. When entering the Earth's atmosphere, these cascades or their components might generate distinct walls of spatially correlated air showers, which could also occur even if the primary photons are not directed towards Earth. Furthermore, it is anticipated that the particle distributions within these multi-photon footprints will possess thicknesses of up to meters and extensions of up to hundreds of millions of kilometers, rendering them potentially observable with a collaborative global approach, incorporating re-evaluation of historical data and exceeding the capacity of even the largest cosmic ray observatories. The methods described in this report enable the simulation of observable quantities related to CRE caused by ultra-high energy photons, such as densities, energy spectra, and particle orientation at the top of the Earth's atmosphere. Additionally, the likelihood of detecting such photons depends on several parameters, including the density of CRE, the energy of the primary photons, and the characteristic length of the solar magnetic field, among others. Modifications to existing multi-photon detection methods are also presented, incorporating the density of CRE and energy of the primary photons as key indicators, along with the implementation of new methods to determine the energy of primary photons and the characteristic length of the solar magnetic field. The techniques described in this report can be applied to identify the signature of ultra-high energy photons, shedding new light on the long-standing problem of solar cosmic ray acceleration. Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to show that de Sitter spacetime does not meet the theory's requirements. Furthermore, the paper derives an implicit equation for spacetime curvature in nonlocal gravity theory. The theory also predicts that a gravitational wave's amplitude is proportional to its frequency and a constant from the specific nonlocal relation used. The paper concludes with an estimation of the nonlocal coefficient based on the recently detected gravitational waves events. The purpose of this paper was explored within the framework of an analog model of nonlocal electrodynamics in curved spacetime. The results obtained are in line with those derived through the direct approach. The implicit equation for spacetime curvature was solved numerically for a specific nonlocal relation used. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' complexity and difficulty to adapt to other data types, there's a clear need for a design framework to facilitate creating new CRDTs with consistency. We propose the RWF, a Remove-Win design framework that utilizes a conflict-resolution approach to update conflicts, allowing its use across various data types. Through two practical applications using Redis, RWF showcases its effectiveness and performance in developing new CRDTs that can handle conflicts efficiently. Furthermore, we highlight the advantages of a conflict-resolution approach over alternative methods, and explore ways to extend RWF to handle more complex conflicts. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. Additionally, we have identified novel targets for resequencing, including a significant proportion of conserved and developmental ly regulated regions and have made available an interactive website with our results. We have also investigated the potential for our approach to be applied to an even broader range of human traits and have found that even without additional data on trait-associated SNPs, we can still identify a substantial portion of the associated SNPs with an accuracy of up to ten percent, with the exception of certain traits such as bipolar disorder and multiple sclerosis. With the ever-increasing wealth of functional genomics data, our approach will continue to enhance our understanding of the genetic basis of complex human traits and diseases. We have made available the statistical approach and results at http://www.broadinstitute.org/research/projects/1000-genomes/. geometric modularity of non-algebraic weights to algebraic weights and vice versa. 
Our investigation demonstrates that non-algebraic weights geometric modularity 
entails geometric modularity for multiple algebraic weights, which has clear 
consequences. Moreover, we prove that geometric modularity of several algebraic 
weights may imply geometric modularity of a non-algebraic weight. This 
connection bridges Diamond--Sasaki's findings to earlier generalisations of 
Serre's conjecture, specifically focusing on weight aspects. 
Interestingly, our analysis reveals that certain weights geometric modularity may 
be related to geometric modularity of all weights. 
The underlying methodology utilizes a combination of techniques, including but 
not limited to, using the geometric Langlands correspondence, the Harder--Narasimhan 
filtration, as well as an approach inspired by the Allcock--Sasaki strategy. 
Additionally, our research introduces a novel application of the geometric 
Langlands correspondence in the context of weight aspects. 
Finally, we conclude this study by highlighting an intriguing open question 
related to the weights geometric modularity problem.

* Rigid geometric modularity for non-algebraic weights implies geometric 
modularity for several algebraic weights;

modularity for a non-algebraic weight;
* The connection between geometric modularity of weights and the weights 
geometric modularity problem;
* The generalisation of Serre's conjecture focusing on weight aspects;
* The application of the geometric Langlands correspondence in the context 
of weight aspects;
* The novel approach to the weights geometric modularity problem.

Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet some challenges remain unresolved. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Given the constraint of limited memory, older classes are learned from fewer examples compared to newer ones, further exacerbating the initial dataset imbalance. Consequently, a scoring bias emerges, favoring newer classes over older ones. We experiment with a comprehensive range of score calibration methods to counter this bias. The evaluation was conducted across three datasets, utilizing two scenarios representing varying degrees of dataset imbalance, and testing three distinct memory capacity constraints. The findings indicate that most calibration methods yield beneficial results, and their effectiveness is particularly pronounced when memory constraints are tighter – a scenario that holds practical relevance. Moreover, our research discovers that incorporating the usual distillation component into incremental learning algorithms is unnecessary. By removing it, a simplified fine-tuning approach emerges as a more robust foundation for tackling imbalanced incremental learning challenges. The complete code used in this exploration has been openly disseminated on GitHub. High-quality videos depicting our experimentation process are available on YouTube. Moreover, a concise paper summarizing our explorations has been submitted to the ICML 2022 workshop on Deep Learning for Dynamic Data, titled “A Comparative Study of Calibration Methods for Imbalanced Class Incremental Learning”. This paper was chosen for an award at the workshop. To determine if the Higgs boson can account for the discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, we employed a bottom-up approach using Effective Field Theory (EFT). Our findings reveal that, given the present experimental constraints on the Higgs sector, its contribution to the anomaly could still be significant, assuming the Higgs interacts non-standardly with other particles. Based on unitarity principles, we found that a solution to the anomaly could imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of roughly 10-18 TeV, which could potentially be as low as 5 TeV if the Higgs' interaction with the W and Z bosons is in line with Standard Model predictions. This outcome may have the added benefit of significantly increasing the rate of di-Higgs production in future muon colliders. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of precisely measuring the Higgs coupling to a muon and itself in forthcoming experiments.

Optimally timing pulmonary valve replacement surgery in Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) patients primarily relies on heart volume and function as per existing medical guidelines. The best indicators for these factors are found through 3D image analysis of the heart obtained from magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging. Recent research involving a type of neural network known as U-Net has yielded impressive outcomes when tested against certain heart imaging data sets, although real-world medical imaging presents unique challenges due to variations in image quality stemming from the specific medical imaging technology used and individual differences in heart conditions. Furthermore, there is a shortage of high-quality, specially tailored data sets for training models on rare conditions such as TOF.

For this research, we first evaluated how accurate models become when they are trained with publicly available, labeled data sets (specifically, the Automatic Cardiac Diagnosis Challenge (ACDC) set) and then tested against CMR data obtained from TOF patients, or vice versa. Then, we sought to find out whether these models could deliver comparable results when tested against a broader data set with more diverse cases. This was accomplished by first training multiple neural networks with four-fold cross-validation before assessing their performance against CMR images that had not been used during training. The findings confirmed that deep learning algorithms can produce exceptional results within the same type of data set (left ventricle precision scores: $0.951\pm{0.003}$/$0.941\pm{0.007}$ for training/validation), but their accuracy significantly declines when they are applied to a different type of heart pathology, resulting in a noticeable gap of $0.072\pm{0.001}$ for the left ventricle and $0.165\pm{0.001}$ for the right ventricle. Additionally, the results indicated that there is a fair amount of variation in scores depending on the specific segmentation used, as well as the difficulty level of the cases, which was objectively quantified using both visual scoring and a newly introduced numerical method. Ultimately, our research failed to detect any significant differences in improvement at higher data sizes (scores: $0.951\pm{0.003}$ for $256$ $xy$ pixels and $0.959\pm{0.004}$ for $512$ $xy$ pixels), but we were able to introduce an innovative method for evaluating the difficulty of cases based on their atypical geometry. The data and models used in this research have been made publicly available to facilitate further exploration of the subject.

A question remains regarding the secondary component of GW190814 - whether it's a neutron star or a black hole of minimal mass. Researchers have introduced an energy density functional, named BigApple, which accurately matches the neutron star's mass of 2.60 solar masses and is in line with GW190814's data. By utilizing BigApple along with four well-established relativistic mean-field forces, a study delves into the characteristics of finite nuclei, nuclear matter, and neutron stars. The predicted properties of finite nuclei and calculated quantities of nuclear matter align well with empirical and experimental values, demonstrating the BigApple parameter set's reliability. Notably, BigApple successfully matches GW190814's data for canonical tidal deformability, while the dimensionless moment of inertia falls within the estimated range based on PSR J0737-3039A's analysis. Furthermore, BigApple demonstrates that the moment of inertia's value can serve as a key indicator in identifying the secondary component of GW190814. With BigApple, the density of neutron stars in the most dense regions can reach 2.43+0.21/-0.19 times the normal density, which has implications for the density of atomic matter in ultra-dense atomic nuclei and quark matter densities in quark stars. Additionally, BigApple predicts a minimum density of 1.37+0.08/-0.10 times the normal density in the most dense regions of neutron stars, which can be verified by future X-ray telescopes such as the Enhanced X-ray Timing Array or the X-ray Imaging Telescope. Researchers also examined the impact of BigApple on the density profiles of neutron stars and found that the radius of a 2.60 solar mass neutron star is approximately 13.85 kilometers, with the density of neutron star surfaces ranging from 1.37 to 2.43 times the normal density. Furthermore, BigApple predicts that the neutron star with a mass of 2.60 solar masses and an equatorial radius of 13.85 kilometers would appear 1.13 times larger than the neutron star with a mass of 1.44 solar masses and an equatorial radius of 12.25 kilometers. Additionally, BigApple demonstrates that the ratio of the equatorial radius to the polar radius, or the ellipticity, of a 2.60 solar mass neutron star would be 1.026, resulting in an elliptical shape that could be confirmed by future X-ray telescopes such as the Enhanced X-ray Timing Array or the X-ray Imaging Telescope.

We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. Notably, this description of frequency robustness offers a promising framework for evaluating and developing resilient gate techniques in trapped ion systems. Furthermore, this demonstration of frequency robustness facilitates the efficient creation of robust states of matter, such as quantum simulators modeling the Huxley protein and certain lattice models. Additionally, this research provides a foundation for further exploration of anti-entanglement gates and the application of 2D molmer-sorensen gates in trapped ion systems.

Lately, researchers have focused intensely on solid electronic theory's strongly correlated systems and graphene, yet the $sp^{2}$-electrons that form Dirac bands in graphene lack strong interactions. Consequently, novel, interaction-induced phenomena tied to Dirac points are underutilized. We propose GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ as a new material where Dirac electrons are paired with strong interactions and frustrated magnetism. Calculations indicate its crystallographic and electronic properties harbor symmetry-protected Dirac points at the Fermi level, allowing for multifaceted physics encompassing possible instabilities of charge, magnetism, or superconductivity. By merging various methods to assess its many-body behavior, researchers have observed potential transitions to Mott-Hubbard, magnetic or charge ordering states, along with $f$-wave unconventional superconductivity in this unique compound. Interestingly, the magnitude of its electronic correlations can be adjusted through small changes in pressure, potentially triggering a phase transition to the normalized Dirac point predicted by theoretical models. Oversaturated electronic competition might also give rise to extreme phenomena such as magnetic Weyl semimetallic or charge ordering states near the critical pressure. Ultimately, experimental verification of this theoretical prediction is anticipated to unlock numerous application possibilities for this novel material. We envision that in the vicinity of the critical pressure, GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ can serve as a parent compound for Mott-Hubbard, magnetic or charge ordering materials or superconductors that can be controlled through pressure, a phenomenon observable in this particular material alone. Nonetheless, the inherent instability of this compound under experimental synthesis conditions poses a challenge to the proposed theoretical model. Fortunately, recent studies have demonstrated the feasibility of obtaining this material at lower oxidation levels, thus the intricate electronic structure and predicted phenomena are expected to persist in an optimized version of GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$. Additionally, this material's unique electronic properties may provide a fruitful basis for incorporating Dirac electrons into strong and fragile quantum states within $sp^{2}$-bonded materials. Experimental validation of this prediction in GaCu$_{3}$(OH)$_{6}$Cl$_{2}$ is anticipated to unlock novel perspectives for the design of electronic systems combining strong and weak interactions. Consequently, researchers should consider incorporating interacting Dirac electrons into $sp^{2}$-electron systems as a promising avenue for discovering unusual physics and versatile applications.

We've developed families of three-dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial, non-toric terminal Fano varieties of considerable depth, corresponding to 54 distinct mutation classes in the realm of Laurent polynomials. From the perspective of mirror symmetry, these high-dimensional non-toric varieties establish the Fano/Landau-Ginzburg connection for our current knowledge limits. Building upon this foundation, 46 more $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds have been constructed, with their depth spanning between 10 and 19. Among these, certain examples will be expressed as toric complete intersections and others as Pfaffian varieties. Notably, one specific variety within the (2,5,7) mutation class possesses the largest known depth among all non-toric, $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial terminal Fano varieties - with a depth of 24. Additionally, several $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds have been found to contain seven distinct mutation classes, thereby expanding our understanding of three-dimensional reflection groups. Constructing upon these $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds, we've derived several $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano four-dimensional varieties by applying the Laurent inversion method - a technique we've introduced here. Lastly, by further analyzing these four-dimensional varieties, at least 52 new $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds with diverse mutation classes will be revealed. The employed method of construction guarantees that these varieties all possess multiple mirrors, which in turn allows us to establish the $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano/Landau-Ginzburg connection for an additional 57 three-dimensional mutation classes. The developed families of $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano fourfolds will in turn produce $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano threefolds with deep complex structure by applying the ball quotient method. The applied technique also yields new complete classification for 12 distinct three-dimensional reflection groups, which in turn will imply the existence of several new $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties of higher dimension. The employed construction method also ensures that these newly created $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano varieties all possess multiple mirrors, which in turn will allow us to establish the $\mathbb{Q}$-Fano/Landau-Ginzburg connection for an extensive number of new mutation classes in higher dimensional spaces. The employed construction method is quite versatile, thereby giving us the opportunity to explore novel areas in the field.

This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our method displays robustness in the face of occlusions, which is further validated by a qualitative analysis of its output. Code is available at https://github.com/zwangseu/SADRNet. Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to designate some right edges as "optional", given they don't lead to leaf nodes. They employed this model to analyze skew Dyck paths. A key aspect studied was the number of deepest nodes in these marked trees. Through explicit generating functions, they obtained insights, revealing the average number of deepest nodes converges to $\frac53$ as the number of nodes increases, which can be contrasted to standard ordered trees with a convergent average of $2$ deepest nodes. Furthermore, the convergence to an extreme value of $n/3$ for the number of deepest nodes was demonstrated, along with a method for identifying the number of nodes at the deepest level using a cumulative product property. This property enabled the derivation of the average number of deepest nodes for a general class of rooted trees. Lastly, the representation of the generating function was also explored through an expansion related to the 5-step move of a Dyck path. Additionally, the accumulation of the cumulative product property was analyzed to determine the number of second-deepest nodes, and an alternating pattern was observed, which further generalized the average behavior under the strict rule scenario. All findings were validated through numerical simulations. Last, the paper concludes by suggesting potential future inquiries related to the deepest node phenomenon observed.

Research has been conducted to evaluate linear models with numerous parameters in high-dimensional environments characterized by non-sparse data. These studies typically assume the independence of data samples, but the current research extends beyond this limitation by exploring a linear regression model with time series data under conditions of over-parameterization, where data samples are inherently interdependent. The study develops an interpolation-based estimator and associated risk theory that accommodates varying levels of data interdependence, infinite data dimensions lacking sparsity, and both short and long-memory processes. The theoretical risk analysis leverages the concept of integrated covariance along with non-degeneracy properties of autocorrelation matrices. The results demonstrate comparable risk convergence rates to those in independent settings for short-memory processes and significantly slower convergence rates for long-memory processes. The research also illustrates specific, applicable examples of dependent processes. It further investigates an early stabilization phenomenon in deep linear models and presents a formal explanation for the Benign Overfitting phenomenon observed in over-parameterized neural networks through the lens of time series linear models. The study's findings are validated through simulations and applications to real-world datasets. The advancement of linear models offers promising prospects for addressing real-world challenges and complexities with statistical models.
