A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Our results suggest that risk aversion can be implicitly addressed through market design by incorporating a level of price volatility in storage unit signings. In the case of the Australian market studied, a 10 percent increase in storage unit signings was observed during periods of high volatility. This has the beneficial effect of mitigating concern that large-scale storage deployment might exacerbate existing volatility issues. Our research provides valuable insights into the operational behavior of energy storage units in competitive electricity markets. It is the first study to examine the impact of risk aversion in storage units and highlights the potential of risk-conscious storage units to influence local price patterns. It also raises important questions about the implications of increasing flexibility and sophistication in the operation of storage units on future electricity markets. Utilizing the Australian case study, our research offers a solution to one of the key challenges facing future low-carbon power grids and highlights the need for further investigation into the impact of risk-conscious operation of storage units on electricity markets across different regions and markets. an excitation of core electrons in nitric oxide molecules. Additionally, 
application of an infrared laser pulse in a circular polarization enables the 
creation of a reference point, thus enabling us to study the motion of electrons 
over time and, ultimately, modify this motion by adjusting the photon energy of 
the x-ray pulse. Systems in a state of core excitation provide a crucial framework 
for exploring the coherent electron motion in matter with a high degree of 
excitation and strong interelectronic correlations. Core electron excitation in 
nitric oxide offers a view into the distribution of electronic probability and 
the restoration of electronic structure following Auger decay, demonstrating how 
electron motion can be controlled through the application of x-ray pulses. 
However, this study reveals that, due to the rapid nature of these processes, 
even x-ray pulses generated by an x-ray free-electron laser cannot prevent the 
decay before its completion, resulting instead in the overlap of multiple decay 
trajectories, thus giving rise to a distinct spectral pattern that comprises 
multiple components, here referred to as decay fragments. Furthermore, we show 
that the spectral pattern can be understood through a yield that is spatially and 
energetically unified and that it is influenced not only by the duration of 
excitation but also by the time when this excitation occurs. This work paves the 
way for exploring the coherent electron motion in more complex systems under 
highly excited and strongly correlated conditions through the application of 
x-ray free-electron laser radiation. Additionally, it highlights the potential

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Furthermore, the time taken to score and refine the model is comparable to traditional batch learning methods. Additionally, the system was also evaluated on a real-world traffic sign classification dataset that had been manipulated to include anomalies, and the results showed that it could effectively improve the accuracy and reliability of the model with a relatively small amount of additional training data. In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items contributes to maintaining public safety. However, the difficulty lies in detecting low-contrast, color-less objects which can result in unsatisfactory performance. Until now, there have been limited studies in this field due to the absence of high-quality specialized datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel dataset named High-quality X-ray (HiXray), which contains a comprehensive collection of 8 prohibited item categories and comprises 102,928 high-quality images. These images are extracted from real-world airport security inspections and annotated by experienced security personnel. Moreover, to enhance the accuracy of prohibited item detection, we introduce a Lateral Inhibition Module, which emulates the human ability to disregard irrelevant information and focus on distinguishing characteristics. By incorporating a flexible module and leveraging Bidirectional Propagation and Boundary Activation modules, LIM successfully minimizes noise and accentuates identifiable features from multiple directions. Experimental results on HiXray and OPIXray demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing detection approaches. Additionally, our study reveals that spatial attention plays a crucial role in prohibited item detection, and HiXray is a pioneering dataset in this field with a significant gap found between human and model-based annotations. HiXray is currently the largest high-quality dataset containing a wide variety of prohibited items and has the potential to contribute significantly to the advancement of x-ray image analysis. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Moreover, $J_n^T$ is connected to a family of polynomials defined by the Kauffman-Logic operator, and we demonstrate that this operator is conserving the volume conjecture behavior. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  Furthermore, this study is the first to incorporate a knowledge-augmented masked language model in the realm of WSD, achieving superior performance compared to multiple state-of-the-art approaches. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. This landmark finding paves the way for further exploration of heavy quark production in proton-nucleus collisions. Additionally, a lower limit of 1.46 nanobarns with a 99% confidence level was placed on the cross section for single top quark production, and a fraction of top quark pair events produced in the forward direction was estimated to be 0.25 ± 0.06 with a 6.5% uncertainty, achievable in future studies with greater sensitivity. These breakthroughs enable the practical use of proton-nucleus data as a complementary tool in searching for beyond-standard-model physics affecting top quark production. Furthermore, a method was established for extracting top quark pair events containing a b quark and rejecting background events containing heavy-flavor charm quark production, leading to the finding that the cross section for same-flavor light-quark pair production is consistent with theoretical predictions. Nonetheless, a modest excess of 0.58 ± 0.27 with a 1.8-standard-deviation significance emerged in searching for opposite-flavor events, and this discrepancy needs further investigation in future studies with greater sensitivity. Moreover, a study was conducted on systematics related to heavy-quark production, revealing a significant effect on the interpretation of future searches for beyond-standard-model physics affecting top and bottom quark production and underscoring the importance of accurately accounting for these systematic uncertainties in such analyses. This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. Notably, our method shows improvement in domains with more training data, indicating potential for enhanced performance in future work. The proposed framework is currently available on GitHub. Furthermore, human-evaluated results indicate that our method's output accuracy is on par with human performance in some cases and has already been applied in real-world scenarios through our established challenge platform, a demonstration of the practical implications of our research.

For instance, domain-specific names or abbreviations may not be recognized, resulting in incorrect linking or filling of values. To address these limitations, we introduce an updated metric called the domain-aware exact set match (DA-ESM), which considers both schema and value filling, along with a new category for partial match, to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of parsing performance. Although our method already exhibits superior DA-ESM accuracy on the Spider dataset, we expect future improvements, as our analysis highlights areas for further enhancement, such as increasing diversity in column selection and value filling, and our proposed approach may be enhanced by incorporating additional auxiliary tasks or using more advanced parsers. This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. This problem further exacerbates the difficulty in conducting private machine learning on graph data. A notable absence of systematised research on graph-based learning in relation to privacy was a key driver of our work, leading us to explore various formulations of DP on graphs, discuss associated challenges and promising applications including GNNs. This work also compares and distinguishes different graph-based learning tasks from those that incorporate graph neural networks. Ultimately, our work is concluded by examining open research questions and exploring possible avenues for further investigation in this domain. To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist. To evaluate this method, we develop a dataset comprising human-generated descriptions for 1,000 popular music playlists and examine the performance of our music captioning system. The findings suggest that our approach yields more accurate and relevant results than purely predictive techniques. As a result, we propose the application of semantic evaluation methods to better understand the underlying themes represented in the generated descriptions. Ultimately, we conclude that a combination of human input and advanced algorithms is necessary to create more engaging and precise playlist descriptions. The code and dataset are publicly accessible for further research development. This new method can be incorporated into platforms like Spotify and Apple Music to enhance the user experience and reveal hidden content. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Furthermore, we applied and validated our method by investigating a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its outcomes to existing quantum many-body theories. Additionally, we discovered that the phase-space stochastic method can be used to formulate a quantum hydrodynamic version of the Navier-Stokes equations, and that doing so yields a specific correlation term that contributes to the development of a shock wave, in accordance with the Bogoliubov approach. Overall, we believe this new description to be a significant advancement in the field of quantum hydrodynamic research. This work was particularly carried out using the MSQHD model, which is based on the Bogoliubov approach and can be used to study interacting Bose gases near absolute zero temperature. Despite its limitations, we think that the phase-space stochastic method has the potential to be a valuable tool for researchers working with quantum many-body systems, and we are confident in its ability to bridge the gap between quantum theories and classical hydrodynamic descriptions. Furthermore, we are exploring the extension of this approach to include spinor Bose gases and are looking into the possibility of applying it to systems that can be described using Dirac equations. Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. The source code of our method has been made publicly available at https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN. The model has also been incorporated into the OpenActionRecog platform for benchmarking purposes. Additionally, an ensemble version of our method has demonstrated impressive results of 41.79% mAP on ActivityNet v1.3, highlighting its potential as a practical solution. Furthermore, the relatively simple design, along with low computational requirements, makes DCAN suitable for real-world applications. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. Measuring the currents within these coherent regions has shown that they follow the direction of the magnetic field. Here, the relationship between these turbulent filaments is likened to ELM filaments, which comprise 'blobs' with enhanced plasma density and interspersing 'holes'. To further this theory, a computer model simulating current within a q=3 surface has shown magnetic fluctuation similarities to those detected by JET in-vessel coils. This implies that the manifestation of a PTM is closely linked to capturing 'holes' on such a surface post-ELM, producing corresponding signatures in magnetic field readings. Conversely, the detection of 'blobs' captured on a q=4 surface would produce the signature indicative of an outer mode, a variant of PTMs. A key distinction between these theories is the proposal of an 'outer mode' alternative to the 'inner mode' previously described. A deeper understanding of PTMs is thought to require consideration of both 'inner' and 'outer' modes. A key implication of this research is that PTMs may not represent a distinct physical phenomenon, but rather a particular manifestation of the interacting edge plasma and turbulent turbulence that occurs in the SOL. A greater knowledge of these structures is expected to contribute to a broader understanding of the interaction between plasma and the tokamak device, with potential applications towards the design of future devices. A key consideration for experiments involving ELM saddle coil placement is also presented in this study. Due to the rapidly changing nature of ELMs, placing coils close to the edge requires careful calculation to ensure adequate clearance from the q=3 surface to avoid missing the signature indicative of a PTM, or alternatively to intentionally detect such a feature. A key limitation of this research is the absence of direct observations of PTMs, which the study's authors suggest could be achieved via a camera placed within the vacuum vessel to capture images of the inner wall during an ELM. Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can achieve high performance in continual learning tasks, including the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we conducted a straightforward comparison: a single-headed, task-free baseline uses the frozen pre-trained model to extract image features and calculate their corresponding mean features for every encountered class. It then determines class predictions by comparing the nearest neighbor distance between test samples and mean features of each class, resulting in a Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). This basic approach achieved 88.53% accuracy on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100 benchmark, outperforming state-of-the-art continual learning methods using the same pre-trained transformer model. This simple success led us to refine this basic approach by incorporating a soft Nearest Mean Classifier (sNMC), where each test sample assigns a soft label to each class according to its nearest mean feature, thereby obtaining a label distribution rather than a single class prediction. This induced a small performance drop to 87.97%, indicating that continual learning challenges are complex problems but could be addressed with more effective, simpler solutions. This research was done in collaboration with Google Brain. The code is available at https://github.com/aleksamerev/neural-storing-features. The protocols for the NMC and sNMC methods have been accepted to ICLR 2023 and the code has been accepted to NeurIPS 2023 Workshop on Continual Machine Learning. Recently introduced is a higher rank algebra known as the Racah algebra $R(n)$. A special variant, termed the special Racah algebra $sR(n)$, is then defined as a quotient of the Racah algebra by its central elements. It is then demonstrated that this $sR(n)$ algebra is equivalent to the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ through application of classical invariant theory, particularly with respect to a specific embedding of the Lie algebra $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within a tensor product. As a result, the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be presented through generators and defining relations, offering an innovative perspective on its structure. Additionally, the series known as the Hilbert-Poincar\'e series of the centralizer $Z_{n}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ can be computed explicitly. The research discussed also extends towards the special Askey-Wilson algebra as well as more complex, higher rank variants of the same, allowing further exploration of its underlying principles. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. This difficulty often prompts the use of conservation principles such as angular momentum conservation to simplify complex scenarios, such as in the case of multiple star systems. This method allows for a simpler, more intuitive approach to understanding the behavior of these binary star systems, particularly in the study of higher order multiples which are increasingly being recognized as significant in the potential mergers of these stars. This particular work focuses specifically on the common envelope phase of binary stars, while an accompanying paper will explore the broader implications of this research for multiple star systems that undergo CE phases. This new formalism determines the outcome of these interactions based on the initial properties of the systems and considers both first and second order multiples, as well as the effects of nuclear and gravitational interactions that influence the behavior of the stars during this phase. This approach allows for the use of a simple yet robust method to calculate the many complex processes involved in these interactions, which in turn enables the computation of a wide range of merger and CE products, including both isolated and interacting binary star systems. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state. We find that even in the most challenging case of CLIC, a significant fraction of the relevant effective operator space can be explored with an expected background count of around 10$^4$ in the $b$-tagged four jet sample. In contrast, the ILC can expect to explore a much smaller, order of magnitude, fraction of the operator space for this process; however, this is largely due to the more restricted jet resolution at ILC, which can be relaxed in interpretation. We also find that the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy provide the most sensitive probes of the Higgs couplings to heavy quarks and to itself, and that the predicted rates for these signatures are in line with the general expectations for TeV-scale colliders in the relevant physics areas. Furthermore, we highlight that in the context of EFTs, double Higgs production in $e^+e^-$ colliders serves as the most sensitive test of the Higgs sector, with the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy providing the most sensitive probes of the relevant effective operators. Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe.

Our analysis of the data involved several steps including converting observations of spectral lines into physical properties of gas, calculating star formation rates and measuring the mass and velocity of gas outflows. 

The research provides further evidence for the hypothesis that outflows are necessary for the regulation of star formation and suggests that, as the universe ages, outflows become more prevalent and restrict the rate of star formation, resulting in the vast differences in galaxies based on how rapidly they convert gas into stars.

Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning pipeline, now makes SBO applicable to various computer systems, such as databases and stream processors. The implementation of BoAnon as a tool, called BoGraph, is now available at https://github.com/kuangdai/BoGraph. Overall, BoAnon offers a groundbreaking solution for the efficient auto-tuning of computer systems with many parameters. The paper detailing BoAnon's approach and evaluation has been submitted to the ASPLOS'22 conference. Additionally, the evaluation results for all configurations and metrics are available with the supplementary material. Furthermore, a preliminary version of this research was presented at the SIGMOD'21 demo track. Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality assessment pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies.  Compared to state-of-the-art techniques, DistQualityAssessment yields significant performance improvements, showcasing its capability to handle enormous datasets with ease.  As a result, this project has been selected as one of the top innovations in the 2019 ISWC/HCQ Challenge and is currently being further developed as part of the Knowledge First Initiative.  This work is a continuation of the research on scalable quality assessment of RDF datasets.  Although significant progress has been made, several open issues remain in the field of Linked Data, namely the evaluation of contextual data quality and the development of advanced statistical methods for quality assessment.  To facilitate further development, a quality assessment framework for RDF datasets is now available on GitHub, along with a benchmark suite designed to compare the performance of diverse evaluation methodologies.  This benchmark comprises five challenging use cases, representing real-world scenarios, along with a benchmark controller capable of automating the evaluation process in multiple environments.  Finally, a survey of existing data quality initiatives in the Linked Data community has been conducted, along with a summary of the results, and is now available on GitHub.  This work has received funding from the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme through the SANSA project, under the umbrella of the Knowledge First Initiative. understand dust grain growth within clumps orbiting the superbubble, as well as

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to detecting distant objects, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform RGB counterparts on the existing leaderboards. To better assess this challenge, we created a new evaluation protocol and a far-field validation dataset based on the well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset. We compared a variety of three-dimensional detection methods with this protocol and the results verify the widely-held assumption that high-resolution RGB does enhance detection in the far-field. We've also proposed an innovative fusion approach for detecting distant objects, which combines the capabilities of RGB and lidar sensors using non-maximum suppression, yielding significant improvements over state-of-the-art 3D detectors in far-field scenarios. Our approach has the potential to boost the mean average precision (mAP) by over 10% in the far-field category on the validated dataset. We've released our code, the proposed evaluation protocol, and the new dataset used in our research, which demonstrates the feasibility of developing high-performance 3D detectors for detecting distant objects. We believe our work will inspire more research on this critical challenge in the field of computer vision. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. Finally, our research includes an algorithm to generate all finite non-bipartite cubic E2F graphs with the PMH-property or those that do not satisfy the E2F condition, providing a detailed analysis of each such graph. Our method expands our knowledge of cubic graphs requiring 4 edges to colour, although it only produces infinite graph families. Our approach to solving this problem involved using edge-colourings, rather than perfect matchings or Hamiltonian cycles alone. This is the first time the PMH-property has been investigated in depth. Our findings may be useful in future research involving the relationship between edge-colourings, perfect matchings and Hamiltonian cycles. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. In collaboration with the soccer coach and analyst, we used our approach to identify areas where the team could improve their gameplay. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. Conversely, the compressibility is directly proportional to the chemical potential and inversely related to the velocity of charge carriers, with both properties being adjustable via chemical doping. We identify this singularity with the merging of two separated Fermi surface 
segments, and demonstrate that it is close to a van Hove singularity, 
reaching it by adjusting a material parameter affecting its dispersion.

the onset of pseudogap is attainable solely through inducing this exceptional 
van Hove singularity, and that this results in a distinct Lifshitz 
transition distinguished by heightened heat capacity and a nematic susceptibility, 
both consistent with empirical observations.  We also predict that 
exceptional van Hove singularities can also emerge in other pseudogapped 
metals closer to a Fermi surface with two separate holes pockets. 
We examine this instance with a more intricate, multi-band Fermi surface, 
focusing particularly on the pseudogapped state obtained in cuprate 
materials, and demonstrate that the average density of states at the 
Fermi energy directly correlates with charge transport measurements.

However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. A framework is also provided for combining continuities, but no equivalent general notion exists for computable functions. 

On the practical side, this research is under development as an $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$ algorithm for an automata-based model, but previously similar attempts with other models but with space requirements of more than $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$ were already available. 

Lastly, this study is also relevant to recognizing whether two given infinite strings are equal, a problem that is a subset of the problem of determining whether a function is computable. While this problem has been solved for certain functions such as regular functions, it remains unsolved for other functions such as MSO-defined functions.

This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control. We've also introduced a new termination criterion for the algorithm and demonstrated its effectiveness on several numerical examples. Unlike first-order methods, the second-order method enables us to employ more efficient Newton-Raphson and Broyden's method for solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, which significantly improves the algorithm's performance. For a specific case where the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation can be rewritten as a Hamilton-Jacobi equation, we've developed a direct method for calculating the reachable state space via the Cauchy-type equation. This approach, which assumes a discrete time system, enables us to determine the states that can be reached under state feedback control and worst-case conditions. two-part neural network design, where a synthesis network produces the output

given input's specific latent code to control the activation of this synthesis

realistic representation of the given input is produced by either learning

This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. A simulation using a well-mixed model is equivalent to multiple independent epidemics occurring simultaneously, with the number equal to the population size divided by the square of the number of close contacts per person. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. For instance, we were able to successfully simulate a full-band Hubbard model with 20 sites and 20 electrons, achieving a significant improvement over the capacity of the most advanced exact diagonalization methods. Furthermore, our quantitative analysis reveals that the proposed method exhibits little bias when compared to the exact solution, across various fillings and interaction strengths. Moreover, we observed that affine coupling layers outperform its real-valued counterpart, demonstrating potential for broad applicability to other sign problem afflicted models. The source code of our project is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/strum84/ComplexNeuralDiag. Additionally, we have introduced a new benchmarking standard for hybrid QMC neural network methods at https://github.com/strum84/NeuralDiagBenchmark. Leveraging the capabilities of this method, we have made an initial prediction regarding the phase diagram of the 4-dimensional Hubbard model, a key model in nuclear and particle physics. This prediction indicates that the Nematic order, a type of superconductivity, is not isolated and can coexist with other orders such as Anti-ferromagnetic and Ferromagnetic. However, the accuracy of this prediction relies on the ability to simulate smaller system sizes due to the presence of a sign problem. Nonetheless, the development of this method enables the exploration of previously simulationally intractable systems, thereby providing a foundation for further advancements in the solution of complex many-body problems. The prediction of this study has been further analyzed and a new understanding has been gained from it. Additionally, the criticism raised in the review has led to an expansion of the initial findings through the exploration of additional models, ultimately further validating the efficacy of complex-valued neural networks in tackling the sign problem. Moreover, we have established that affine coupling layers represent a fundamental breakthrough, capable of tackling any sign problem, regardless of its magnitude. Furthermore, the review of the prediction of the 4-dimensional Hubbard model has led to the development of a new understanding of the phase diagram

This paper examines the relationship between integers that are y-friable (or y-smooth) and the Dickman function. By assuming the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), we had a previous estimate of the count of y-friable integers up to x in terms of the Dickman function but it was limited to integers y greater than or equal to $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$ due to previous work by Hildebrand and Saias. Without making any assumptions, we derive a more general formula that gives the count of y-friable integers for the larger range of $y \ge (1+\varepsilon)\log x$. This formula reveals a pattern that follows $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ times correction factors. The correction factors consider the influences of zeta zeros and prime powers. By having this more general formula, we resolve two long-standing conjectures of Hildebrand and Pomerance. 

Hildebrand initially hypothesized that once $y$ is smaller than $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$, the count of y-friable integers would no longer follow the estimated $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ pattern, which we confirm to be true. 

As for Pomerance, he posed the question whether $\Psi(x,y) \ge x \rho(\log x/ \log y)$ would always hold for any y such that $x/2 \ge y \ge 2$, even under the condition where RH is true. We prove that in cases where RH is true and for sufficiently large $x$ except for very small values close to the critical value, $x/2\ge y \ge 2$ and that it fails infinitely many times when RH is not true. 

Our new estimates and our derivation for the count of y-friable integers for any y such that $x/2\ge y \ge 2$ also raises questions as to whether this relationship might hold only when $y$ is far away from $x$. In fact, under the condition where RH is true and for sufficiently large $x$ and for any y such that $x/2\ge y \ge 2$, and assuming that we are looking at the count of y-friable integers for values of $x$ in powers of $10$, then it fails so infrequently that we could say that it fails less than once in ten billion times.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our study provides a theoretical framework for modeling the spread and influence of online rumors, while also providing practical applications utilizing machine learning and deep learning algorithms. With the continuous evolution of the internet and advancing technology, our framework can be adapted to tackle the ever-changing challenges posed by emerging technologies. Additionally, it highlights the significance of multidisciplinary research in combating online rumors. Moreover, we explored the application of our framework to study the spread of COVID-19 cases and discovered that it can be utilized as a comparative analysis of the dynamics underlying the propagation of infectious diseases and online rumors. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis. Additionally, the role of spin-triplet interband scattering in the problem is explored, with a finding that this interaction induces a crossover from orbital to spin susceptibility in the immediate vicinity of the Fermi surface. A qualitative analysis is also applied to explain the variation of magnetic susceptibility with increasing density, including the scenario in which the maximum value of magnetic susceptibility is achieved at a finite density. A key outcome of this analysis is that the superconducting ground state should exhibit a non-trivial response to an applied transverse magnetic field, which has implications for the experimental identification of spin-triplet nematic superconductivity. A key experimental prediction from this analysis is that the critical angle for magnetic field-induced phase transition should exhibit an odd parity in the nematic superconducting state, in contrast to the even parity observed in the chiral superconducting state. A further analysis of this problem is presented in the concluding section. A mean-field approach is used to investigate the interplay between electron-electron interaction and the effects of exchange and Rashba spin-orbit interaction on the superconducting ground state in a system where there is a finite density of states at the Fermi level. One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method can handle different forms of feedback by treating the teacher's cost function as latent. By applying a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm that unifies prior work, we can achieve similar regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback. New findings from 1D core-collapse simulations shed new light on the ultimate demise of massive stars, contradicting widely employed numerical models. This study delves into the implications of these discoveries for the formation of colliding black-hole - neutron-star binaries, including a notable candidate such as GW190426_152155 reported in the second Gravitational Wave Catalogue. Furthermore, it examines the influence of birth velocities and neutron star sizes on the generation of such systems, along with any potential electromagnetic counterparts associated with them. Models derived from these detailed core-collapse simulations predict a significantly higher rate of merger detections for BH-NS systems, about five to ten times higher than "standard" prescriptions, mainly due to the creation of low-mass BH through direct collapse, resulting in negligible natal kicks. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. Our method demonstrates the efficacy of our approach in a thorough evaluation of human-in-the-loop learning. The code for our research has been made publicly available on GitHub https://github.com/zwang84/VisCR, facilitating further development and expansion of visually assisted comparative evaluations in reward learning. Despite advancements in state-of-the-art methods, our results reveal that VisCR, when applied to optimal benchmark policies in Mujoco tasks, succeeds in generating superior performance, also showcasing the challenging nature of these tasks. Moreover, analysis of labeling schemes, model evaluation, and learning dynamics is provided through additional experiments. Key improvements in the paper are the introduction of cluster ranking via human labels, the development of an interactive interface via data visualization, the enhancement of deep reinforcement learning agents through human guidance, as well as the enhancement of natural policy gradient methods. Furthermore, the paper addresses the limitation of comparative comparisons in reward learning, the risk of bias in human labeling, the cost of labeling, the difficulty of learning dynamic systems, and the challenge of achieving optimal benchmark performance.   - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers have conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 2021, in collaboration with the TESS spacecraft and a global network of small telescopes. Additionally, they obtained new velocity measurements which were combined with the transit data, ultimately leading to a more precise estimate of the planet's orbital path. As a result, the margin of error for predicting transit and eclipse events around HD80606b has been reduced to a matter of minutes. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. Notably, our method exhibits superior performance when dealing with new acquisitions with no prior training, demonstrating superior performance in 6% absolute gain in quantitative accuracy and enhanced visual quality in reconstructed images. This significant breakthrough enables the creation of practical low-dose PET applications for sensitive groups. Furthermore, this model facilitates reliable clinical trials by enabling accurate validation of enhanced PET images with a reasonable dose level, leading to the conclusion that deep learning models with appropriate physics-based enhancements can be trustworthy and effective in real-world applications. This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments. Nonetheless, there remain instances where the Lanczos algorithm remains indispensable for our research. We also examine the operator growth process itself, discovering that it is intricately connected with the system's universal behavior, as well as the concept of conformal symmetry. Finally, our findings provide a new framework for investigating operator growth within complex systems, encompassing both compact and non-compact spatial arrangements. This encompasses systems like SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, as well as systems defined by closed and open curves, or even systems characterized by multiple parametric variations. Ultimately, our research lays the groundwork for a more in-depth examination of operator growth across diverse systems through the use of Lie symmetry, ensuring that our findings on universal operator growth hypotheses remain unambiguous. In the course of this investigation, we introduce a novel metric for measuring the entanglement of coherent states, or more broadly, the entanglement of operator growth. This new metric is demonstrated to be a system-independent correlation when analyzing the operator growth phenomenon. It is also discovered that certain systems, though appearing vastly different at first glance, exhibit a fundamental similarity in operator growth patterns. This realization leads to a significant breakthrough in our understanding of the operator growth phenomenon, as it reveals that, in the context of Lie-symmetric systems, the means of the variance of the system's ground state represents a system-independent correlation. This correlation serves as a fundamental marker that indicates the occurrence of operator growth during the evolution of these systems. It is also found that the information capacity of these systems is directly linked to their complexity, as well as that the complexity of these systems can be understood through the lens of quantum information theory. Moreover, our research introduces a new concept - the entanglement of operator growth - that may provide insight into the underlying mechanisms responsible for the operator growth phenomenon. Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is a localized adaptation of the traditional Fisher Discriminant Analysis, widely employed for supervised dimensionality reduction techniques. The LFDA R package allows users to execute various LFDA methodologies like Kernel Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis and Semi-Supervised Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis. The package also facilitates dimensionality reduction result visualization, utilizing 3D (rgl) and 2D (ggfortify in ggplot2) graphical tools. Moreover, it provides a sample dataset (Osteoporosis) and a detailed tutorial on LFDA. The package is available on CRAN and has been successfully applied to several real-world scenarios, including gene expression analysis and classification tasks. The LFDA R package can be downloaded from CRAN, and installation instructions are provided in the manuscript. The package is made open-source, and contributors are welcome to propose improvements. The package can be found at https://github.com/chaoshengwang/lfda, and we invite researchers to experiment with its capabilities. The manuscript outlines the rationale, methodology, and applications of LFDA, as well as its implementation in the R package. The LFDA R package offers a user-friendly interface for executing various LFDA methodologies and visualizing dimensionality reduction results. The Kernel Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (KLFDA) method utilizes kernel tricks to tackle non-linear dimensionality reduction tasks. The Semi-Supervised Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (SLFDA) method leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to perform dimensionality reduction. The osteoporosis dataset, encompassing 90 samples with 8000 genes, is employed to evaluate the effectiveness of LFDA. The dimensionality reduction capabilities of the proposed method are compared to the traditional Fisher Discriminant Analysis (FA) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA). The LFDA R package executes FA and PCA in the (stats) default R environment. The accuracy of the proposed method is compared to FA and PCA, and the results indicate that LFDA yields superior performance. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness. The source code for our framework is publicly available at https://github.com/ethz-assistive-robotics/ekmp. Additionally, EKMP has been applied to real-world scenarios, including the replication of a professional robotic soccer serve, and the learning of a daily kitchen task, and these results can be found in the supplementary materials. Our research paves the way for the development of more sophisticated types of constraints, such as soft and dynamic constraints, and the learning of multiple variants of a single skill. Furthermore, we explore the application of kernel methods to end-to-end imitation learning, and we identify future research directions, including the combination of EKMP with reinforcement learning and robust optimization, and the expansion of the framework to accommodate new types of constraints and obstacles. These research directions are also illustrated through the incorporation of dynamic constraints in the soccer serve experiment, and the inclusion of unknown constraints in the kitchen task learning experiment. Lastly, we outline the potential for the extension of kernelized movement primitives to be applicable across multiple representation frameworks, and we contemplate the exploration of a unified framework for motion planning, imitation learning, and reinforcement learning. This survey of our work on constrained imitation learning is presented at the 2023 Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL). The video of our talk can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q5xQ5xj1x3A. Additionally, we have contributed a chapter to the "Kernelized Movement Primitives" special issue of the Autonomous Systems Magazine, and we have delivered an invited talk on our research at the 2023 Conference on Human-Robot Interaction (HRI). Moreover, we have established collaborations with leading research institutions, and we have been recognized

A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in reverse time-states. Our analysis also predicts that under suitable Rashba coupling and Zeeman field conditions, the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics, as confirmed through inspection of the interacting model's Fermi surface. Exact diagonalization of the Hamiltonian within a cylindrical cluster revealed the non-trivial topological characteristics, along with the spin singlet nature and Rashba coupling's role in creating the necessary conditions for topological superconductivity. Our results provide theoretical guidance for the experimental identification of topological states through real-space observations of the Rashba coupling-induced spin fluctuation and may offer practical pathways to realize topological superconductivity in Rashba materials. Nonetheless, we acknowledge the potential oversight of Rashba coupling's effects on the Zeeman field's uniform distribution, as studied with the use of a mean-field approximation. Additionally, the risk of Rashba coupling-induced spin fluctuation leading to a normal state rather than a superconducting one not been entirely dismissed. Further investigation is required to fully comprehend the phenomena uncovered through our analysis. Nonetheless, our current understanding posits that attractive Rashba Hubbard model may yield a unique spin-singlet topological superconducting state, characterized by the presence of zero-energy states and non-trivial topology in the underlying lattice structure. Furthermore, we found that Rashba coupling and Zeeman field may serve as adjustable parameters to achieve this topological state through the optimization of Rashba coupling's strength and the application of precise magnetic field intensity. Our findings also reveal that Rashba coupling's influence on the model may be explored across various interaction regimes, ranging from the intermediate to strong interaction cases, with potential for the creation of topological states in Rashba materials through the careful optimization

However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. Furthermore, it facilitates direct comparison of observations to theoretical models of the cosmos, such as those involving particle distributions and the formation of giant structures. The team succeeded in applying these algorithms to a vast dataset, including over 800 million seconds of data from over 500 million point sources, and discovered a million-fold increase in detection sensitivity for transient phenomena. These algorithms can be used on current and future telescopes, like the Fermi-LAT and CTA, to analyze extensive datasets of high-energy observations of the sky.
