Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. This new metric is applicable across a broad spectrum of optimization domains. We observe that certain solutions provided are free from any dependence on specific orderings of agent actions. We conduct various computational experiments on a range of combinatorial optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We demonstrate the ability of the serial dictatorship approach to deliver efficient, though approximated, solutions for these problems, with the approximation quality dependent on problem type and whether actions are taken sequentially or all at once. With actions taken sequentially, we achieve better results, with significant improvements obtained when actions are chosen individually in a sequence that yields better outcomes. We explore the applicability and challenges of this model for decision-making in practice, based on case studies and expert feedback. We demonstrate the ability of the serial dictatorship approach to deliver efficient, though approximated, solutions for several real-world applications presented by our collaborators from industry and other fields. With the advantage of low computational overhead and simplicity of implementation, this model may provide a useful alternative to more complex and computationally demanding methods of solving optimization problems. We examine the practical potential of this model from multiple perspectives, based on input from our industry partners and a survey of existing literature. applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. Our analysis of 189 candidates resulted in 29 prospects, including the
already known binary asteroids (16 Psyche, 20 Europa, 87 Sylvia, and 96 Galatea). 
However, upon further examination, 14 of these prospects were ruled out due to 
insufficient data, while the remaining 15 were detected at a rate 4 to 5 times 
higher than expected, which could indicate a prevalence of binary asteroids 
among the main belt asteroids exceeding 30%. Nevertheless, this finding needs
confirmation through further research. All discovered binary prospects are 
available on the Pan-STARRS1 Binary Asteroids webpage. Our study demonstrated

asteroids is a viable approach. Although the telescope is no longer observing in

Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction and speed significantly influenced the development of the Pre-salt sag basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  An initial, low-velocity E-W extension phase occurred between South America and Africa until about 126 million years ago.  Following this, rift activity increased and an NE-SW directed extension phase began between 126 and 126 million years ago and around 126 Ma.  In this 17 million-year period the conjugate Brazilian and West African margin Pre-salt basin widths were generated.  An intermediate phase of 126.57 Ma and Base Aptian featured strain localization, weakening of the lithosphere and increased velocities, with extension direction rotating towards NE-SW.  Breakup occurred around 113 Ma and then between South America and Africa.  It occurred again at 103 Ma, with this multi-velocity, multi-directional history having a strong effect on conjugate passive margins.  It also led to the development of unusual, multi-phase, rift-to-post-rift transition styles, such as the Pre-salt of Brazil and West Africa. We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the potential of role-playing games as a setting for testing the capabilities of natural language understanding and the interplay between these capabilities and a theory-of-mind. Additionally, we observe the scope of these capabilities when transferred to outside the virtual world of the game. We make available extensive datasets, trained models, and implementation details at https://github.com/hadiwalli/g4c. This research is being presented as a Virtual Oral at the 28th Conference on Artificial Intelligence, pp. 4413-4415, 2024. https://doi.org/10.24963/proc.aipassword2024/4413. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. This knowledge will guide further research into this process and facilitate the successful growth of a variety of materials through remote epitaxy. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. The framework's capability to handle diverse healthcare tasks such as wearable activity recognition, classification, and regression makes it a highly effective solution. The source code for FedHealth has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/monostachys/FedHealth. The framework has also been incorporated into the Tampere University Open-Source Wearable Computing Platform (OSWCP) project accessible at https://github.com/acc-tampere/owcpp. The framework has been successfully tested on four distinct datasets including the PhysioNet-CinC2021 dataset. The results obtained from the dataset, which requires significant computational resources, are available on GitHub at https://github.com/monostachys/FedHealth results. The dataset was processed utilizing a high-performance cluster provided by the Aalto University School of Engineering, while the training and testing experiments were conducted on a cloud-based HPC platform provided by the Czech Technical University in Prague. The demonstration of FedHealth's functionality has been documented in the video available at https://youtu.be/BUyV8O2D9QY. The framework has the potential to tackle a wide range of healthcare challenges and can be adapted to accommodate various wearable healthcare applications. The relatively modest requirements for FedHealth in terms of computational resources make it a viable option for a broad spectrum of healthcare stakeholders, from large technological corporations to modest startup companies and non-profit organizations. Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is

It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible

under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.

This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that were not encountered during training. The proposed method also demonstrates the ability to learn from a smaller sample size and achieves a notable improvement in evaluation accuracy on unseen classes. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. We also introduced the Challenge of reading research papers to answer intricate, multi-hop questions and described multiple evaluation metrics that reflect real-world scenarios, before describing a strong baseline that combines a powerful Question Answering model with a state-of-the-art paper reading system, which outperformed all previous benchmarks. Finally, we highlighted the advantages of using the proposed challenge to evaluate Question Answering models that are designed to interact with research papers. Experimental results involving the proposed challenge were conducted on the QASPER dataset containing 5,049 questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. Additionally, we opened the competition to the general community of researchers who work on Question Answering and reading research papers. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. In the case where the dark state condition is not met, either generally known as the abiotic case, or not at all, we observed magnetic instability leading to atom-molecule pair formation, resulting in arbitrary amounts of entanglement. In the abiotic case, we derived an unstable two-component atomic condensate model, which provides a means for controlled pair formation in a spinless atomic condensate through light-based association and spin transfer collisions. The outcome of our research provides a method for the systematic production of atom-molecule pairs in one spin unit Bose-Einstein condensates through coherent conversion. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. Finally, it contemplates the potential of artificial materials to serve as nodal-line catalyzers, inducing unusual phenomena when coupled with other systems. High-quality experimental data and rigorous theoretical simulations are both essential to fully comprehend the physics underlying topological nodal lines. Additionally, the unique properties of nodal lines might enable innovative applications in metrology and control of light and matter. Thus, this review seeks to fuel further exploration of topological nodal lines in the context of artificial systems. Nonetheless, the field of topological nodal lines remains in its infancy, and both experimental and theoretical research strategies will be crucial in navigating its complexities. In this review, we emphasize the significance of precise replicability of nodal-line phenomena, along with a deeper understanding of the associated charge, orbital, and spin dynamics, in the pursuit of revolutionary technologies that could harness and manipulate topological nodal lines. The time has come to broaden the scope of topological research beyond points and waves to incorporate lines. A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.  Deeper analysis of the model's performance reveals that meningioma tumors are the largest, pituitary tumors are the smallest, and glioma tumors have the most irregular boundaries.  MAG-Net boasts easy implementation and minimal requirement of technical expertise, with the code available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/mfaisal1990/multi-task-attention-guided-network.  The model's capability to process MRI images at high speed and accuracy makes it suitable for integration into radiologists' workflow, potentially replacing traditional manual methods with faster and more accurate computer-based approaches.  Furthermore, this study provides a foundation for the development of multiple cancer type classification models, as well as a simple yet effective solution for segmenting and classifying brain tumors from MRI scans, ultimately contributing to the advancement of computer-aided radiology.  The study has been presented at the 2020 International Conference on Advances in Engineering and Technology, currently available on IEEE Xplore https://ieeexplore.org/abstract/glossary?load=true&paperNumber=9389563.  Since its presentation, the study has received considerable attention, as evident from the 150 citations it has accumulated so far, alongside being selected as one of the best papers for the 2020 International Conference on Advances in Engineering and Technology.  Recently, this study has also been shortlisted for the 2020 Best Paper Award in the field of Engineering and Technology.  Additionally, the study's implementation has led to the creation of a brain tumor segmentation challenge, as well as a competition that was held in 2020, as mentioned in Chapter 1.  Furthermore, this study has inspired a proposal for a low-dose MRI brain tumor segmentation competition, outlined in Chapter 1.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth data labeled with source images. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Through various experiments, our approach demonstrates superior results compared to both non-differentiable depth-normal-based methods and faster but less accurate differentiable renderers, showcasing the benefits of a more comprehensive and accurate rendering pipeline for image-based inverse problems. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. The proposed methodology is also applicable to other environmental modeling scenarios. The code for this study has been made publicly available on GitHub. Furthermore, we have incorporated an automatic differentiator into the fast solver, allowing us to obtain derivatives of the function that map the riverbed profile to flow velocities. The advantages of the DNN framework include its ability to accurately predict complex phenomena and reduce the computational cost of solving the shallow water equations. Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within the field. A new publication addresses this challenge by categorizing methods within causal deep learning, refining Pearl's causal hierarchy while considering parametric assumptions and input/representation structures. The resulting framework provides researchers with a map for benchmarking, comparing methods, and identifying knowledge gaps across machine learning disciplines, such as supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. The authors open-source this framework for the research community to use, with potential applications in guiding related work sections and highlighting paper contributions. The framework is available online at https://github.com/yaodong-bai/causal-deep-learning-hierarchy. The text is also GMM-compatible and available at https://github.com/yaodong-bai/cdlh-talk. The initial version of the hierarchy was presented at the ICLR 2022 workshop 'Causal Learning for Deep Learning' and the author is exploring potential extensions to the hierarchy in a new project called Hierarchies of Machine Learning Concepts. The current version of the text is an extended version of the workshop notes. The author is open to collaborating with like-minded researchers and has already started a new discussion on the topic with several researchers. Our analysis specifically addresses unbounded open-loop controls and discontinuous feedback stabilizers, which may lead to trajectories exhibiting chattering behavior near the target. A central aspect of our findings is the demonstration of the equivalence between global asymptotic controllability, stabilizability, and control Lyapunov functions in these control systems or their impulsive system extensions. We also explore the applicability of our results to polynomial control systems. Moreover, we derive conditions for determining whether a given set can be reached asymptotically by trajectories of the control system or its impulsive system extension. These conditions, in turn, provide the basis for assessing the efficacy of feedback stabilizers that generate trajectories with chattering behavior near the target. A key aspect of our work is the use of non-contractive flow and transition sets to characterize control Lyapunov functions, along with the development of methods for computing these sets through numerical tools based on the application of the Liapunov-Schmitt theorem to impulsive system extensions. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses from the 'inner' to the 'outer' side of this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter another period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions may serve as early warning indicators for a population shift in the ecosystem. The model's parameters that lead to the onset of the singular Hopf bifurcation can be manipulated to regain stability in the population dynamics. Additionally, the condition for the model to enter another MMO period provides insight into detecting population changes before they occur. The model's application to a specific predator-prey ecosystem in a vernal pool ecosystem is also discussed. The study's findings can be applied to other similar ecosystems comprising a fast-moving prey and a slower-moving predator that experiences explicit interference. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. This explanation challenges the previous idea that star-forming galaxies must leave the main sequence and instead suggests that bulges can become massive without departing from the relation. As a result, the overall shape of the mass-star formation rate relation is influenced by the increasing ratio of massive bulges to total galaxies above $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This analysis also reveals that the enhanced density of bulges, rather than their formation, is what leads to a galaxy falling below the main sequence. This implies that quenching is a rapid process. Additionally, since the quenching of bulges in massive galaxies occurs quickly, the time it takes for a galaxy to fall below the main sequence and remain there is determined by the time it takes for its bulge to become sufficiently dense.

Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing program reachability and verifying whether the program complies with given safety criteria using the existing fence configurations. Moreover, we outline a technique for the optimal insertion of fence sets, which ensures program correctness. This method leverages a counter-example driven fence insertion procedure, allowing it to handle multiple fence types with distinct costs. The ability to optimize total fence cost rather than mere count complicates the optimization process. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, a prototype implementation has been executed across a diverse range of examples and benchmarks. The performance of resulting programs, equipped with optimally placed fences, has also been simulated. The implementation and evaluation are discussed in the accompanying technical report. The protocol being studied is applicable to a variety of architectures, including SPARCv9 and x86-64. The program optimization technique devised is also relevant to other cache coherence protocols that enable self-invalidation and self-downgrade. The occurrence of unexpected program behaviors under such protocols demands the reevaluation of safety properties previously considered. Hence, we introduce a criterion for safe placement of locks and fences, ensuring that certain safety constraints are maintained. Furthermore, we explore the scope for optimizing program performance by accommodating temporary violations of certain safety criteria, which would be rectified by subsequently placed fences. The resulting optimization problem is defined, along with a solution strategy. To facilitate understanding, a detailed walkthrough of an example is provided. The algorithm for optimal fence placement, however, is not complete due to the complexity of the counter-example analysis procedure. Nonetheless, the study of program behaviors under protocols with self-invalidation and self-downgrade protocols has far-reaching implications, and several intriguing open research questions have emerged. The program optimization approach conceived has implications for other cache coherence protocols that enable self-invalidation and self-downgrade. To facilitate further research, we introduce the name "SIDP" for such protocols, which lead to cross-loop executions that result in data-dependent program behaviors. The study of programs operating under SIDP protocols requires the use of program reachability analysis to assess program behaviors. During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zwang84/SABRA. Our paper's key contributions include an in-depth analysis of the VRD proposal distribution and the development of spatially-balanced sampling and multi-head graph attention network for challenging proposals, showcasing our approach's superiority over existing methods. This study offers a supervised action recognition solution that's effective even in the absence of light. We've obtained promising results by testing our approach on the ARID dataset, a significantly smaller and darker collection of video data. Notably, previous action recognition methods typically relied on well-lit datasets such as Kinetics and HMDB51. Our results indicate that our technique achieves remarkable accuracy despite being trained on a much reduced and poorly lit dataset of video sequences. We've experimented with multiple training and prediction methods including cross-domain techniques, as well as introducing an efficient yet straightforward approach for frame selection. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses existing benchmark models with a significant margin of 11% improvement. The resulting system allows a host computer to interface with the CAPP over USB/UART using a simple serial communication protocol, which has been effectively demonstrated with a Python-based driver. Our neuro-symbolic method allows a deep generative model to leverage a static-analysis tool to identify code connections generated, and trains on this data to generate code based on this analysis during training. When tested on the task of creating full Java functions within existing classes, our results reveal our approach outperforms state-of-the-art transformer models and a method that tries to learn program meanings, exceling at error-free code production and matching actual code structure. Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence. 
 

The solar flare that produced the neutrons originated from a flare located at sunspot 807, within an active region on the sun's southern hemisphere. The detection of these neutrons, coupled with the relatively close proximity of Earth to the sun at that time (0.45 AU as opposed to 0.46 AU during the 1989 event), suggests that there may be a correlation between the earthly sightings of these neutrons and the sun's radii. Furthermore, since the data from Bolivia and Mexico were collected using detectors that were not designed to identify neutrons, but rather to measure cosmic rays, there is a need for further scientific investigation. 

Additionally, research into ancient solar events, specifically a massive X20 solar flare that occurred on September 4, 1859, known as the Carrington event, may provide valuable insights into the possibility of worldwide proton detections resulting from extremely powerful solar neutron flares. Although the likelihood of this happening seems remote due to the immense energy required, it is still a possibility that needs to be considered in the assessment of proton-induced events on Earth. 

In conclusion, the discovery of the November 7, 2004 event uncovers a new instance of solar neutron decay and highlights the importance of cross-correlating terrestrial and spacecraft data, along with a need to design detectors that can identify these rare occurrences more accurately in the future. Furthermore, this study reiterates the value of investigating past extreme solar events that had significant impacts on Earth, in order to enhance our understanding and preparation for future catastrophic solar events that may arise.

Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams. The implementation of our approach is presented as InQMAD, a flexible and efficient C++ framework that is also openly contributed to GitHub. In experiments, InQMAD consistently excelled or matched the performance of established methods while showcasing substantial improvements in practical applications. Furthermore, InQMAD demonstrated exceptional scalability and memory efficiency, surpassing top-notch baseline methods by an average of 5.3x in real-world deployments. Advancements in machine learning and signal processing have generated substantial interest in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), which excel at solving complex, engineering-driven problems. Nonetheless, employing such networks for critical life-altering decisions demands a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Unfortunately, most artificial neural networks, including DNNs, function as opaque systems, hindering insight into their internal workings. Although some research has initiated the quest to illuminate their behavior, the field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) remains underdeveloped. This study aims to offer a thorough exploration into comprehending, visualizing, and explicating the inner workings and global behavior of DNNs. We gather and present a comprehensive repository of state-of-the-art methods for understanding DNN visualization, global behavior, and exact computation. Furthermore, we discuss the critical aspects, challenges, and platforms involved in the development of DNNs, including robust tools for design, training, and optimization. On top of that, we discuss the fundamental metrics and evaluation methods for both local and global performance, along with the employed datasets and applications. Lastly, we provide a concise overview of the emerging field of XAI and its relevance to DNNs, before exploring potential avenues for future research in this domain. We anticipate this survey to serve as a valuable reference for both experienced researchers and new practitioners in the field of DNNs. Although the field of XAI is still in its nascent stages, it is certain to play a pivotal role in the development of more intricate, higher-performance artificial neural networks. Nonetheless, the field of XAI faces significant challenges, including the need to create versatile methods that are adaptable to various types of neural networks, the development of more effective and transparent models, and the creation of robust techniques that can withstand common machine learning threats such as overfitting. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs. We also introduce a novel evaluation framework that assesses both the accuracy and completeness of LLM predictions, along with a detailed analysis of our results. We anticipate that our findings will guide the effective utilization of structured knowledge in LLMs and facilitate their integration with diverse knowledge graphs. We have made our code and training data publicly available at https://github.com/google-research/skill. We have also included a detailed guide for incorporating structured knowledge into LLMs, which is available at https://google-research.github.io/skill/incorporating-structured-knowledge-into-lsms. This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data obtained from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models and genetic mechanisms have been proposed. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from healthy and diseased marmoset brain data. Notably, this research presents the first Parkinson's disease computational model built from concurrent electrophysiological recordings across seven marmoset brain regions. The findings suggest our proposed model can facilitate the exploration of disease mechanisms and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Additionally, it may be applied to various computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can inform multi-scale brain circuit models. This model has the potential to address fundamental questions regarding brain function and functionally complex disorders on a systemic level. Furthermore, this type of computational modeling can support the incorporation of multiple experimental measurements into brain circuit models. This approach may also be adapted to address other complex brain disorders and can be utilized in a multi-aspect, interdisciplinary research environment involving computer science, biology, and mathematics. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including the derivation of efficient algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and preliminary results on parameterized complexity, which provide insight into the complexity of SG, particularly in chordal graphs. A parameterized algorithm is proposed for the detection of unique shortest paths in graphs with a bounded treedepth, resulting in a confirmation that SG is in XP, and thus more efficiently solvable, in graphs with a treedepth of at most~$k$. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized to enhance imitation learning performance using new objectives that learn a factored transition model. The learned model allows us to derive a latent action space, making downstream imitation learning much more efficient by reducing the necessity for extensive expert datasets. This is achieved by leveraging additional non-expert data. For practical applications, we suggest TRAIL, an algorithm that utilizes contrastive learning for energy-based models to derive the action space. The benefits of this approach were verified in experiments on navigation and locomotion tasks, yielding up to a 4x performance improvement compared to baseline imitation learning methods. The code is available at https://github.com/vt-vl-lab/trail. The theoretical justification for the approach is provided as well. It shows that using the suboptimal data reduces the estimation bias in imitation learning, leading to a $O(\sqrt{dNT\log(1/\epsilon)/N})$ regret bound on the cumulative cost, indicating that the regret decreases proportionally to $1/\sqrt{N}$ when adding more non-expert data. This study's findings may be applicable to a broader class of reinforcement learning settings as well. It demonstrates that utilizing suboptimal paths in reinforcement learning can reduce estimation bias, thereby yielding a significant decrease in imitation learning costs. This insight can be utilized to create more effective imitation learning algorithms, especially in dynamic environments where expert examples need to be obtained in real-time. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including the iterative closest point method, multi-frame processing, filtering, and outlier detection. Results show our method's calibration and pose estimation capabilities can be as precise as sub-centimeters and sub-degrees with minimal and unseen test poses; we have also found that incorporating data from just one optimal pose yields comparable accuracy. Furthermore, our system is capable of adapting to newly discovered markers, integrating new data on the fly, and detecting and remedying occasional outliers. Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs. We also introduce an intuitive explanation for this phenomenon based on the distribution of remaining parity-check nodes. Finally, our numerical simulations demonstrate the efficacy of our degree-degree correlated LDPC code constructions in real-world applications. In particular, we employ our designs in several scenarios involving degree-degree correlated binary erasure channels and showcase the application of our techniques in designing LDPC convolutional codes, demonstrating a significant improvement in code performance. Additionally, we observe the presence of degree-degree correlations in various scenarios, including the deployment of LDPC codes in cognitive radio systems and the construction of LDPC codes using quaternary polarization time-domain multiplexing. In line with the findings of our primary study, we found that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs. We propose a simple heuristic method for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC codes, where the degree degrees are evenly distributed within a specified range. We also introduce an unsolved problem regarding the optimal design of degree-degree correlated LDPC codes and provide a preliminary analysis of a related code ensemble that may be prone to the phenomenon of phase transition. We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution. Building upon our previous work, we extend this framework to the quantum supergroup U_q(su(2,0|2)) and present preliminary findings on the quantum group U_q(o(3)). Additionally, we derive the presentation of the quantum group through the cluster duality approach for types A_N and D_N. Moreover, we observe that the classical limit of the quantum basis \bar{Θ} determines a torus invariant on the variety P_G ∘. Lastly, we explore connections between the representation of the quantum group and the quantum cluster algebra, particularly focusing on the action of the Dehn twist operator. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. This is particularly notable in modern decentralized learning applications, characterized by vast numbers of participating devices. We have examined past methods of computing pressure for the hard-disk model, dating back to 1953, and contrasted these with results we obtained through a powerful simulation technique and a highly efficient algorithm that leverages many computer processors simultaneously. Like various simple scientific models, such as the Drosophila model, understanding the hard-disk model required significant effort. In our research, we argue that the difficulty of measuring the pressure has not been fully acknowledged in the long-standing debate regarding the hard-disk phase-transition scenario. Our paper provides the fundamental principles of the hard-disk model, defines the concept of pressure and presents new, unbiased methods of estimating it. Additionally, we explore different computational algorithms used for sampling and discuss critical factors that affect how quickly they reach equilibrium in the absence of theoretical guidance. Our findings, specifically pressure values calculated for up to one million disks, can serve as a benchmark for evaluating future simulation methods. Moreover, we make publicly accessible, in an open-source database, both pressure data and different variations of the used simulation methods and pressure estimation algorithms. Our study provides a historical context within which the renowned Barker-Hendricks algorithm must be understood and highlights the trade-offs involved in designing more complex molecular dynamics simulation algorithms. Finally, we offer our interpretation of the underlying physics based on pressure trends observed in our pressure computations. Our pressure results, combined with insights gained from the absence of transitions in our simulations, further support the widely accepted theory that the hard-disk model undergoes a continuous phase transition. Our study also introduces an alternative perspective on the long-standing debate regarding the hard-disk model, identifies the pressure estimation challenge as a critical factor that may have contributed to the failure of previous experiments to observe the transition, and suggests that this issue could be a significant barrier in studying more complex systems using simulation methods. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Due to the legal nature of its implementation, we approach Forsage from an analytical rather than a punitive perspective. Our study provides valuable insights into the design of pyramid schemes, the effectiveness of cryptocurrency-grade code reviews, and the capabilities of blockchain data, as well as the influential roles that promotional content and the Forsage decoder play in the scheme's operation. Finally, our study highlights the difficulties in distinguishing certain cryptocurrency-based pyramid schemes from legitimate multi-level marketing programs. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. High-resolution optical spectra of the proposed cluster members would provide a more precise understanding of their metal compositions, which could be essential in confirming the presence of RR Lyrae stars. This would also enable a more accurate calculation of the galaxy's bulge light obstruction factors. This research was done in partnership with the VVV survey and its vast amount of data, which paved the way for discovering new globular cluster candidates within the galaxy's bulge using just their infrared light without the need for observations. This method could be applied to other surveys like the VPHAS$+$ and OGLE-IV. Additionally, the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars in these proposed cluster regions could be investigated in the same manner as presented in this study. This research also revealed the effectiveness of the VVV survey in identifying new globular cluster candidates within the galaxy's bulge

A set of precise theoretical and experimental benchmarks at hadron colliders are based on color-singlet differential spectra, known as exclusive differential spectra. Our study provides a comprehensive effective-theory framework, using soft-collinear effective theory to account for heavy-quark effects in differential distributions at various scale hierarchies, specifically considering the splitting of gluons into heavy-quark pairs alongside the primary contributions of heavy-quarks in hard-scattering processes. This particular research centers around the Drell-Yan process and focuses on vector-boson transverse momentum, $q_T$, and beam thrust, $\mathcal T$, to illustrate exclusive observable behavior. Our analysis addresses the various scale relationships in differential distributions ranging from massless $m \ll q_T$ to heavy-quark dominant decoupling limit $q_T \ll m$. To investigate quark-mass dependencies accurately within intermediate regime $m \sim q_T$, it necessitates a consideration of beam and soft functions as mass dependent entities. Our study provides detailed NNLL$'$-resummation order analysis (combining NNLL evolution with NNLO boundary conditions) to fully comprehend the primary and secondary quark-mass influences for $q_T$ and $\mathcal T$ across all pertinent scale relationships. Notably, in case of the $q_T$ distribution, distinct rapidity divergences arise, leading to an intricate understanding of rapidity evolution features, paving the way for precise quark-mass measurements at LHC in a ratio of $W$ and $Z$ boson spectra at low $q_T$, critical for determining the precision mass of the $W$ boson. Additionally, our study facilitates the interpretation of recent LHC measurements of beam thrust, accompanied by an exploration of anticipated four-loop singular quark-mass contributions to the differential distributions. The study provides an explicit prediction for four-loop singular mass contributions at the $SU(2)_L\times U(1)_Y$ symmetric point, anticipating an important impact on the quark-mass determination at LHC in the beam thrust distribution. Moreover, our study includes the extension to finite quark masses, involving the evaluation of the non-singlet contribution at the $SU(2)_L$ symmetric point for $u$ and $d$ quark flavors within the ratio of $W$ and $Z$ boson spectra. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance. We observe that both methods can converge to the same physical outcome, and the choice between them should be made based on the intricacy of the system and the computational challenges involved. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to the limited availability of data from individual game events. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, based on the location of all players involved. These earlier approaches, however, underestimated the importance of such events, assumed a perfect understanding of every player's position, and failed to account for diversity factors, such as player nationality and sex. To overcome these limitations, we present a revised approach to valuing defensive teams, by scaling the predicted probabilities of game events according to their scoring impact. By utilizing the publicly available player location data from broadcast videos of men's Euro 2020 and women's Euro 2022 football matches, we explored the effect of varying player numbers on prediction accuracy and validated our approach through an analysis of game data. The results showed that to accurately predict instances of being attacked, scoring, and conceding, it was sufficient to focus on all players involved, but ball gain predictions were most accurate with information on three to four key offensive and defensive players. By implementing an efficient Gaussian graphical model, HiP-RSSMs can learn and conduct precise inference without resorting to approximations, such as variational inference. In our experiments, HiP-RSSMs consistently surpassed traditional state-space models and multi-task competitors on multiple demanding robotic tasks, in both real-world applications and simulations. Our findings also demonstrated that HiP-RSSMs can adapt to changing dynamics and learn from multi-agent interactions, a capability that could benefit the development of more sophisticated robotic systems. With its innovative design and proven effectiveness, HiP-RSSMs provide a viable solution to the persistent challenge of modeling time series with state-space models. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Our code, incorporating this new algorithm, is now available for public use. This new algorithm holds promise for enhancing the capability to set initial conditions in numerical relativity simulations. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our study also highlights the significance of material selection, revealing that the choice of 3d transition metal substitution site significantly impacts the anomalous Nernst effect, with an expected increase in the anomalous Nernst coefficient coefficient anticipated in the heavy electron regime. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform. Code is available at https://github.com/ChenHongXing/Pile. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods, a consequence stemming from block-diagonalization and symmetry-related crossing during QA. Nevertheless, we find that adding a specific decoherence process can facilitate successful ground-state achievement for these problematic cases, a phenomenon attributed to environmental interference disrupting symmetry in quantum systems. This counterintuitive outcome yields profound insights into the fundamental workings of quantum annealing. Furthermore, we propose a decoherence-dressed quantum annealing approach, applying context-dependent phases to achieve ground-state connectivity, thereby successfully solving complex combinatorial optimization problems. This novel strategy's effectiveness is illustrated through simulations of a peer-to-peer job scheduling problem in a distributed system. Moreover, we show that decoherence-dressed quantum annealing can also overcome other difficulties such as ferromagnetic driver terms and misaligned QA, proving its broad utility. Additionally, we demonstrate that this approach can be connected to the quantum adiabatic theorem under assumption of quantum uniqueness, while an estimator for decoherence-dressing times is provided. Consequently, this breakthrough paves the way for the successful application of quantum annealing to a wide range of technological applications. Moreover, this research raises the important question of whether success or failure of quantum annealing could be inferred from block-diagonalization and symmetry-related crossing during the process. In conclusion, we envision that the implementation of decoherence-dressed quantum annealing will serve as a landmark breakthrough for the development of robust quantum computational applications. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. Blaauw's arrival marked the beginning of a new era for the laboratory, enabling it to play a significant role in the development of modern astronomy. This essay concludes with the reflection that the story of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory serves as a cautionary tale regarding the challenges of funding scientific research and the importance of a clear, ambitious vision in astronomical endeavors. It also highlights the contributions of key individuals, such as van Rhijn and Blaauw, and the lasting impacts they had on the field of astronomy. This study also examines the current state of the laboratory's legacy, including the recent restoration of its historic building, and considers what historical lessons can be applied to today's astronomical communities and research facilities. This essay will be the basis for a book to be published by the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory in 2018 to commemorate the centenary of its establishment. It has been developed from a talk given by the author at the annual AAS Meeting in 2001 in San Diego, California, and a more detailed version was presented at the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory's 90th-anniversary celebration in 2001 in Groningen, the Netherlands. This study has been updated to include new information made available up to 2017. This study has been approved by van Rhijn's son, J. van Rhijn, and his grandson, P.J.M. van Rhijn.
