Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
The potential of this methodology to contribute to the development of more accurate damage detection algorithms and a deeper understanding of the multifaceted behavior of self-sensing materials at different damage levels is also demonstrated. 
However, a noticeable limitation of this study has been the disregard for the effects of conductive fillers at the interface, which, according to the research, could be a significant area for exploration. 
Furthermore, both the theoretical and experimental approaches can be adapted to address the challenges associated with other complex problems involving the measurement of varying cross-sectional areas, such as the assessment of bone density. 
In the case of bone, a more precise measurement of its density could be achieved by incorporating an internal reference point, which could be complex to implement due to the unique characteristics of bone, which is significantly different from the materials used in the composites studied in this research. 
In conclusion, the research has successfully demonstrated the capability to develop an accurate, physics-based algorithm that could effectively solve one of the major limitations associated with the use of self-sensing materials, which could now be applied to a wide range of composite materials, as well as other complex systems, and could also be used as a platform to investigate the effects of different fillers, the behavior of materials under different failure modes, and the development of more precise damage detection algorithms.

We have designed a novel control method using learning algorithms for complex systems whose behavior is unknown. This algorithm excels in environments where there is only limited, high-noise data from ongoing experiments. It achieves exceptional results by making the most of various types of secondary information about the dynamics, such as basic physical laws and the system's general properties. The algorithm essentially finds the best possible solution to an optimization problem by gradually refining a dynamic system model that incorporates unknown components. This model is based on streaming data from ongoing experiments. The algorithm uses a method to predict all the possible system outcomes and establish a theoretical limit on its performance when the actual dynamics are known. The study shows that providing the algorithm with more side information or trial data results in tighter performance guarantees. The algorithm's effectiveness is confirmed by simulations on advanced flight simulator and video game-like environments, and the experiments demonstrate comparable performance to machine learning algorithms that are trained over vast datasets. Notably, the method outperforms existing techniques combining dynamic system modeling and optimal control methods in the tested scenarios. The study also examines the extent to which the performance guarantees hold when the given data is inaccurate. The method is applied to control a quadcopter in a realistic simulation, and the findings indicate that, in some cases, the performance can approach the guaranteed level when the side information accurately represents the actual system dynamics. This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Comparative analyses between each pair of demographic groups within the same semester, and between groups across semesters, were conducted to identify significant differences in student performance. In addition, exam and course scores in Fall 2020 were compared against those of the Fall 2019 semester, and against demographics groups. Findings showed that remote learning led to a decline in on-time and early module submission rates among first-generation students, but resulted in increased early submission rates among transfer students. Under-represented minority students demonstrated enhanced engagement with modules, while non-URM students exhibited similar levels of engagement before and during the pandemic. These outcomes highlight the varying effects of remote learning on students from different demographic backgrounds and underscore the importance of adaptable instructional designs that cater to the unique needs of a diverse higher-education student population. Furthermore, the research sheds light on the lasting impacts of remote learning on students' learning habits and emphasizes the necessity for revised assessment frameworks that acknowledge the differences in learning habits among students from varying demographic groups. Additionally, the study suggests the utilization of corrective instructional designs, such as phased learning assessments and phased learning content, to address the persistent effects of remote learning on students' ability to stay on track. The research also offers recommendations for the implementation of rigorous control groups and the collection of explicit demographic data in future studies. Moreover, the investigation recommends the exploration of design-based research and quasi-experimental research designs to study the effects of remote learning on students' ability to stay on track. The study further recommends the consideration of additional demographic variables, such as disability status and age, as well as the examination of cross-disciplinary learning outcomes. The research also suggests the utilization of implicit and explicit measures of demographic variables, as well as the exploration of machine learning techniques to identify demographic variables. All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by a Lie algebra based path integral formulation. This document is intended to outline the means through which this higher level of symmetry is exhibited within a probabilistic framework that was rigorously introduced by Rhodes, Vargas, and the first author. A distinguishing aspect of this framework is the presence of holomorphic currents, which are derived via a precise derivation of the Miura transformation. Notably, we demonstrate that the spin-three Ward identities, which embody the principles of higher-spin symmetry, are applicable in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. This proof relies on an initial set of explicit expressions for the descendant fields, which are otherwise unidentified within the physics literature. This representation of descendant fields enables the development of a novel method for systematically identifying degenerate fields in both the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda and Liouville conformal field theories. Consequently, this implies that certain four-point correlation functions are solutions to a specific third-order hypergeometric differential equation. This connection between Toda conformal field theories and Lie algebras is further highlighted by the presence of a conserved density, which results in a modified differential equation for the four-point correlation functions. This study is an extension of the earlier work presented in the paper titled "Ward identities in the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Toda conformal field theory" by the same authors. A more comprehensive understanding of Toda conformal field theories is also derived from their relation to Virasoro conformal field theories, which is utilized to determine the specific four-point correlation function quantities that are identically equal in both theories. This identification of common correlation functions serves as a foundation for further investigating the underlying relationship between these conformal field theories. This investigation includes a demonstration of the explicit connection between the descendant fields in both the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda and Liouville conformal field theories, which is derived from the implicit expressions for the descendant fields. This implicit representation of the descendant fields is equivalent to the explicit expressions provided in the physics literature, which is confirmed by a comparison of the two. This study provides a comprehensive answer to the question of what constitutes a degenerate field in both the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda and Liouville conformal field theories.

Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. The algorithm is simple to implement and outperforms state-of-the-art methods, including Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation, according to our comprehensive experiments conducted across up to 128 GPUs. This insight is valuable for both cloud center administrators and users, highlighting the need to mitigate network noise and address scalability concerns when designing large-scale HPC applications. This research can serve as a foundation for further exploration into optimizing cloud-based HPC deployment, along with the development of strategies to handle network noise and scalability challenges. Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. Our results demonstrate the reliability of all key constructs and the validity of all hypotheses, while also highlighting the advantages of combining home working and Scrum practices through an IPMA analysis. Notably, supporting employees' inherent needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness is crucial in the remote working context. Our findings indicate that both home working and Scrum use contribute to project success, with Scrum playing a mediating role. Additionally, we discovered the Scrum values serve as a bridge between home working and project success, while our results also reveal the limitations of our study using data from software engineers. Our recommendations for practitioners and future research are outlined, along with the implications of our findings in the face of the ongoing pandemic and anticipated post-pandemic challenges. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our algorithm has the potential to significantly accelerate particle-resolved simulations of sediment transport and other particle-flow interactions. Additionally, we observed that the standard method can result in the development of unstable waves at the interface between particles and fluid, whereas our algorithm suppresses this phenomenon, providing further insight into the behavior of particles in turbulent fluid. Our study confirms that accurately modeling particle collisions is crucial and has a significant impact on the simulation of complex fluid-particle interactions. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for the displacement of the terrain during the robot's movement, the system was modified to include a control-oriented model. This resulted in a more precise feedforward force control system. The RFT-based model was simplified to include the velocity-dependent damping of the robot and the terrain. This led to the creation of a closed-loop control system using a proportional-integral controller. The demonstration of the one-legged robot's ability to jump on yielding terrain paves the way for the exploration of more complex terrain dynamics and control systems in legged locomotion. This research is a response to the prevalent method of testing legged robots on firm, non-yielding terrain and highlights the need to incorporate ground reaction forces that account for the deformation of soft terrain in the design and control of these systems. This project is a collaboration between robotics researchers and mechanical engineers. It is proposed that further investigation into the modeling, simulation, and control of legged robots be conducted through a working group on dynamic systems. This project involves the collaboration of multiple institutions and presents an opportunity for graduate students to work on a significant project. This includes the development of a one-legged robot platform, the creation of a simulated environment using DEM, the derivation of resistance force models, the design of a feedforward and proportional-integral controller, and the modification of this controller to account for the deformation of soft ground. This project could be expanded to explore more complex terrain dynamics and control systems in legged locomotion. Although previous research has thoroughly analyzed the complex interactions of a liquid droplet under an electrical influence in air, the droplet's effects on the surrounding gas phase have been underrepresented. A notable phenomenon arises when the droplet undergoes significant oscillations, induced by the presence of a resonating electric field. The air circulation patterns that emerge as a result create localized aerodynamic forces that impede the droplet's ability to attract particulate matter in its vicinity, especially when the droplet is immersed in an aerosol cloud. The interplay between the droplet and its surroundings sparks curiosity in scientists, who see the potential for further discoveries in this two-phase system, encompassing both gas and liquid components, especially with regards to the transport of heat and mass. This report showcases the findings of an experiment conducted with a droplet electrohydrodynamic blower in an aerosol-filled environment. The experiment involved a water droplet, suspended in an aerosol cloud generated from nicotine, placed within a sealed chamber under an electrical field. The resulting data, obtained through both direct observation and analytical techniques, provided a spatial and temporal analysis of the produced aerosol cloud, revealing the droplet's influence on both the gas and liquid phases through the creation of a circulating air current. This led to a significant increase in the nicotine's evaporation rate around the droplet, resulting in the formation of a localized area with reduced nicotine concentration. This phenomenon was further validated through both theoretical calculations and experimental data, which demonstrated a droplet electrohydrodynamic blower's capability to circulate air and accelerate the evaporation of a liquid in an aerosol cloud. This discovery may lead to a better comprehension of various phenomena, such as the diffusion of droplets in the atmosphere and the evaporation of liquid droplets within an aerosol cloud. This knowledge may also be applied to develop new methods for dispersing nicotine in nicotine delivery systems and could provide a basis for further exploration of the interactions between gas and liquid phases in a droplet electrohydrodynamic blower. This report concludes by outlining potential areas for research in this field, specifically focusing on the behavior of a droplet electrohydrodynamic blower in different environments and the development of new formulations of nicotine delivery systems. This could involve both theoretical and experimental studies of a droplet electrohydrodynamic blower in various settings, as well as the creation of advanced nicotine delivery systems using a droplet electrohydrodynamic blower. This report also discusses the implications of a droplet electrohydrodynamic blower on the evaporation and distribution of liquids

Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. Our expectations are that this dataset will propel the development of cutting-edge NLP models capable of accurately interpreting and drawing inferences from negated statements. We anticipate that these models will eventually translate to better performance in more applied datasets that frequently incorporate negation, thereby enhancing the efficacy of these models in real-world applications. To accelerate the advancement of such models, we also introduce a novel evaluation metric called consistency, which provides a clear indication of a model's ability to draw inferences from context and negation scopes. We experiment with multiple model improvements, introducing the Consistency-Aware Question Answering task, along with the results of our investigations into the effects of negation scopes, in-order strategies, and the incorporation of negation cues, which offer valuable insights for both researchers and practitioners. Finally, to facilitate the exploration of various techniques for enhancing the performance of NQA models, we publicly release our implementation of these methods, which we anticipate will facilitate further discoveries in this domain. We confidently believe that CONDAQA will serve as a landmark challenge for the NLP community, propelling the development of models capable of accurately processing negation and, in extension, complex language, thereby revolutionizing the way in which human and machines interact

extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon.

$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging.

this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band

which arises solely from this single model.

arising from this two-band model holds the potential to provide a deeper
understanding of recent experimental findings, specifically those involving the
Kondo-lattice-like behavior observed in infinite layered nickelates.

the electron-electron and electron-lattice interactions that are pivotal in
determining the nickelates' structural and magnetic transitions as well as
pairing mechanisms.

atomic-like $s$-band may serve as a starting point for structural distortions
and additional correlation effects may result in an extra pair of $s$-like orbitals
self-doping with $d$-weights, leading to a possible transition to a
self-doped, antiferromagnetic ground state.

arrangements surrounding isolated sites and the fact that in infinity layered
nickelates, there are indeed non-bonding, isolated electron states located at

This allows for solitons to be moved from a stationary state by incorporating invariance. Researchers face a challenge in finding models capable of exhibiting stable, self-accelerating motion of solitons. Self-accelerating modes are well-documented in linear systems in the form of Airy waves, but these waves exhibit poor localization. This concise analysis presents a pair of two-component Bose-Einstein condensate models which can accurately predict the existence of self-accelerating solitons. One such model, featuring interacting 1D solitons, involves a binary BEC trapped within an optical-lattice potential and utilizes interaction forces with opposite signs to create an equilibrium where both solitons accelerate equally. Meanwhile, the total momentum remains conserved. Another model, derived from Gross-Pitaevskii equations for resonantly-coupled atomic components using a microwave field, facilitates an exact transformation to a moving frame of reference, thus providing predictions for one- and two-dimensional stable self-accelerating solitons, including vortex rings. These models offer unprecedented outcomes, including the propagation of a soliton ring supported by an azimuthally-polarized light and a self-accelerating plane-wave mode in a dual-condensate mixture. These discoveries may also lead to the identification of self-accelerating modes in other systems governed by nonlinear Schrödinger equations. Additionally, this study demonstrates that invariance plays a crucial role in the creation of self-accelerating states. This is made possible by an appropriate choice of the coordinate and momentum operators in the moving frame of reference, effectively bypassing the constraints of this review, which only considers applications of this approach to models described by the Gross-Pitaevskii equations. This analysis also highlights the benefits of utilizing the'slow-time' method in conjunction with the 'gauge' approach to solve the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, as this results in a vast expansion of our understanding of self-accelerating modes in condensed-matter physics. Finally, this study paves the way for exploring other applications of Bose-Einstein condensates governed by the Gross-Pitaevskii equations, including their interaction with light in optical lattices and photon condensates formed using laser fields. An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  However, the research acknowledges limitations in its ability to determine whether treatment caused the decrease in crime or if it was simply associated with other factors such as less severe offenses at the time of sentencing.  An attempt was made to address this by controlling for the original offense as well as incorporating a instrumental variables approach in which the decision to refer a defendant to a mental health facility was influenced by the facility's availability and location.  Although the alternative methods yielded similar results, the data still has limitations in terms of data availability and the specific time period studied.  Furthermore, the research extends beyond North Carolina as the state's court case database provides detailed information on the offenders, the original crime, and the treatment received at a county level, allowing for local and state-level analysis.  Additionally, the research explores the effect of mental health treatment on future crime within the broader criminal justice system in North Carolina between 2001 and 2015 using a more aggregate approach with similar results.  The study also examines the change in recidivism rates and treatment coverage pre and post-adoption of evidence-based guidelines in North Carolina and finds that prior to adoption, individuals receiving mental health treatment had a 6 percentage point lower chance of recidivism, and with the adoption of these guidelines, this effect increased to a 11 percentage point lower chance of recidivism.  The data also indicates an increase in treatment coverage as well as a decrease in racial disparities in receiving mental health treatment following adoption.  The results of the study provide strong evidence that mental health treatment reduces future crime and subsequent arrests, and the data suggests the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub. 
  Results on ACDC showed an average Dice coefficient of 0.792±0.033 for 10-fold cross-validation with only 12 labelled images per segmentator, while the best previous score was 0.753. 
  For the MMWHS dataset, with only 5 labelled images per segmentator, the average Dice coefficient for 10-fold cross-validation was 0.823±0.0112, surpassing the current state-of-the-art in semi-supervised medical image segmentation. 
  The method has been successfully applied to segment multiple organs across various anatomical sites with little to no overfitting. 
  Compared to model-based methods, it has the advantage of not requiring extensive memory and computational resources. 
  The simple design of the proposed method allows for the incorporation of prior knowledge, such as symmetry and connectivity constraints, through the use of suitable interpolation methods.

To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake a major upgrade to the LHC's detector system. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize finer details of the data, courtesy of the Feature EXtractors (FEX) system. Specifically, the jet FEX (jFEX) system aims to enhance jet identification and calculate global variables within an extremely tight latency constraint of under 400 nanoseconds. This will involve six distinct modules, where each module on an ATCA board contains four high-end Xilinx FPGAs to process the data at an astonishing 3.6 terabytes per second rate. This ATCA board utilizes an array of components such as electrical-optical devices and multi-gigabit transceivers for data transfer, as well as a custom 24-layer PCB to minimize interference while maintaining high signal integrity. This project has successfully overcome design hurdles and has demonstrated its performance capabilities with the fully assembled final prototype having achieved up to 12.8 gigabits per second during in-house and CERN integrated testing. With production scheduled for completion by the end of 2018, the full jFEX system will be ready for deployment before the LHC's anticipated 2021 restart. This project serves as a prime example of the feasible integration of complex digital systems into particle physics detectors. This work was initially planned for presentation at the 2018 IEEE Nuclear and Plasma Sciences Meeting but was later included in the proceedings due to unforeseen circumstances. This paper provides a detailed technical overview of the jFEX system and its associated ATCA board in the context of the ATLAS detector upgrade for the LHC. Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. Furthermore, we prove that if $M$ is comprised of a single compact component $X$, then the kernel of $P$ consists of functions that are constant across $X$. This is accompanied by an extension of the classical result of Weyl's lemma, stating that if $P$ maps $C^\infty(M)$ to $C^\infty(M)$, it first identifies functions vanishing on $X$ before determining those that are entire on $X$. This in turn enables an extension of the classical result of Titchmarsh's theorem to manifolds. Finally, we also establish an extension of an interior estimate for solutions to elliptic equations. These results are all also shown to generalize previously established facts. This includes the fact that first-order elliptic operators are surjective on compact manifolds, a fact that was previously proven by a different method by the second listed author. These lectures were later recorded and uploaded to the website of the conference. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. Furthermore, a communication-relevance analysis indicates that the algorithm's convergence depends on the degree to which communication promotes convergence, and a threshold exists to ensure convergence certainty. Simulations validate the algorithm's effectiveness, and it is suitable for various applications, including non-deep models and training multiple models simultaneously. The code is available online.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments. This includes the phenomenon of spatially uniform breaking patterns, where the size of clusters remains the same even when we change the rate at which we are stretching the raft. A model of this type also successfully explains the behavior of rafts that are being stretched at the same rate in different directions (tensile flow). Furthermore, we have observed in our experiments that when we stretch a raft in only one direction, deeper clusters will break apart more easily due to the uneven distribution of forces within the raft. This effect can be adjusted by changing the rate at which we are stretching the raft, or the properties of the fluid the raft is floating in. This knowledge could be applied to better understand the breaking patterns we see in more complex systems that are made up of clusters of cells, like tissues in living organisms, or in dry sediment at the bottom of a body of water. Additionally, we have successfully applied our technique to study the breaking patterns of monolayers that are floating in air, although the clusters in these systems tend to be much larger and take much more time to reassemble once they have broken apart. A model of this type also successfully explains the behavior of these systems, although the forces at play are a bit different, with neighboring particles moving apart due to the contraction of the surrounding gas rather than expansion. These scalar fields are part of the fundamental representation of both the SU(Nc) gauge group and the global U(Nf) symmetry group. We've investigated their interactions within a general quartic potential that is compatible with the global and gauge symmetries. By analyzing minimum-energy configurations and performing Monte Carlo simulations, we've studied the phase diagrams, Higgs phases, and corresponding symmetry-breaking patterns. The influence of the quartic potential has also been considered. Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments. In particular, we aim to identify the lowest required comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with limited depth. Specifically, we found the smallest k that allows a sorting network with depth d = 1, 2, 3, or 4. We found that k is equal to n for d = 1 and 2. Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the analysis of isothermal magnetization revealed a unique 1/3 magnetization plateau, corresponding to an 'up-up-down' arrangement of the Gd3+ ions. A notable increase in magnetic entropy was also observed in the GdInO3 system, originating from the inherent magnetic frustration within this compound. A model incorporating a classical spin Hamiltonian was employed to develop the theoretical phase diagram, showing a ground state dominated by weak easy-axis anisotropy and closely resembling that of an equilateral triangular-lattice system. Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, an experimental technique, to detect dark matter. Unlike conventional detectors, which require massive and expensive set-ups, paleo-detectors utilize naturally occurring rocks with deep geological history that contain tiny damage tracks from dark matter interactions. Thanks to advancements in microscopy and the ability to study samples over billions of years, paleo-detectors can potentially offer more sensitive detection at significantly lower costs. This could significantly expand the range of sensitivity in dark matter research. Using updated analytical methods, scientists have simulated the capabilities of paleo-detectors under various conditions and found them robust against inaccuracies in age measurements and the composition of samples. Even with relatively high concentrations of radioactive contaminants, the sensitivity of paleo-detectors can surpass current limits, offering the possibility to detect dark matter interactions below existing detection thresholds, even when masses are less than ten GeV. The sensitivity of paleo-detectors also depends on the duration of the cosmic time exposure, but it starts to saturate at around one billion years. Furthermore, paleo-detectors can offer unique insights into interacting dark matter particles that could affect planetary stability by scaling up existing searches. Additionally, scientists are exploring the possibility of using paleo-detectors to detect other rare events, such as neutrino interactions and dark energy interactions, and they believe that even a small increase in sensitivity could have significant implications for fundamental physics questions. However, there are several technical challenges that need to be overcome before implementing paleo-detectors, including accurately measuring the age of samples, calibrating the detection methods, and containing the statistical uncertainties. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Simulation results demonstrate this scheme offers enhanced spectral efficiency, particularly in scenarios with higher signal-to-noise ratios. Furthermore, the proposed scheme is applicable to frequency-division duplex systems. Overall, this approach offers an efficient solution for the downlink feedback problem. We also explore the impact of varying the number of GMM components and feedback bits, examining how these parameters affect performance and codebook construction. The results suggest that, although increasing the number of components or feedback bits generally improves performance, it does not offset the performance gain from the proposed scheme over traditional methods. The code for this study has been made publicly available. Moreover, the paper includes an analysis of the computational resources required for training the GMM. Although the proposed scheme requires more computations than traditional approaches, the cost can be managed with a suitable compromise between performance and complexity. We examined two alternatives to the GMM-based codebook, including a simpler model with reduced parameters and a robust alternative using a different statistical model. The former fails to deliver comparable performance, whereas the latter yields better results but demands more computations. The paper concludes by outlining potential directions for further research, such as exploring new computational methods or examining the applicability of the proposed scheme to full-band systems. The case for using a GMM-based codebook and feedback encoding approach has been presented, and the results show this scheme delivers enhanced performance over traditional methods. Although the proposed scheme requires more computations and higher feedback bits than traditional methods, it achieves better performance, and the computational cost can be managed with a suitable compromise between performance and complexity. The study provides a starting point for the design of large-scale antenna systems, and the results demonstrate the potential benefits of applying machine learning techniques to codebook construction and feedback encoding. The fact that the proposed scheme performs better than traditional methods suggests that adopting it would result in better spectral efficiency in actual systems.

Two-dimensional systems with robust edge currents due to large Chern numbers offer a wealth of chiral modes related to their topological invariants. In photonic configurations, these edge currents translate to stable multi-mode waveguides that naturally protect the topological properties of the system. In our research, we combine these photonic setups with quantum sources, using a Harper-Hofstadter model to illustrate scenarios where quantum emitters display nearly quantized emission rates. These increased emission rates can result from interactions with multiple edge modes within different energy gaps. Notably, we find that spontaneous emission from these sources can separate spatially, creating time-bin entangled states upon applying a single control pulse. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of emitters selectively interacting with distinct channels via light-matter coupling. These capabilities provide the foundation for implementing quantum operations among protected photons and generating complex, entangled states of light within these topological channels. In essence, we demonstrate that topological quantum electronics can provide a secure and robust platform for manipulating light-matter interactions at the quantum level. In the complex context of an urban intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge: generating safe pathways for automated vehicles. Our research focuses on preventing rear-end collisions when a connected vehicle's human-driven leader approaches the yellow and red phases of the traffic light. We've developed a predictive control system that can instantly forecast how the preceding human driver operates and utilize this prediction to create a safety-oriented pathway in a limited timeframe. The performance of this framework has been tested using a simulation and we assess its reliability. Furthermore, we investigate the convenience of adding data from various human drivers and discovered that although it improves the accuracy, it also increases the computational demands. Finally, we confirm that our developed approach exceeds the capabilities of existing human driver models. The parameters of the controller, such as the forecasting and computation time horizons, were selected based on optimization of several criteria including safety, comfort, and their combination. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. As part of this project, we identified and incorporated several cutting-edge techniques for enhancing performance, including the use of multi-threading, a more effective random number generator method, and a significant optimization of virtual environment creation. We have openly released the source code of our improved simulations and incorporated it into a leading evaluation framework used to assess the skills of virtual agents in text-based tasks. We included results from benchmark tests conducted on both the original and optimized versions of these simulations. Furthermore, we explored the influence of different simulation speeds and game difficulties on the performance of virtual agents. Finally, we used this opportunity to examine the reliability of results obtained from evaluation studies conducted on text-based games through self-play, a well-established method used to assess the capabilities of virtual agents. We provided a validation approach designed to ensure the validity of any conclusions drawn from such studies. Additionally, we introduced a new benchmark used to evaluate the effectiveness of methods proposed to enhance the performance of virtual agents in text-based tasks. We expressed this new benchmark in the form of a text-based game that can be solved using different strategies, and we included results from experiments conducted with several state-of-the-art virtual agents. We released this new benchmark, along with all results and methods presented in this paper, to the public at large. We also included an analysis of the results obtained from experiments conducted with state-of-the-art virtual agents on three widely used text-based game challenges. We provided a summary of the advancements made to each of these challenges and included an assessment of the reliability of the performance achieved by these virtual agents when tested on these optimized simulations. We concluded by outlining several challenging problems in text-based games that solution methods proposed in this paper did not address, and we introduced a new problem-solving approach designed to tackle some of these challenges. Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests. In particular, on the ActivityNet v1.3 dataset, the FDHT-LSTM model achieves an accurate detection rate of over 30% with a model size of merely 4.5MB, representing a considerable enhancement over the  memory-intensive  baseline  and  other  compressed  models.  In  terms  of  energy  efficiency,  the  proposed  FDHT-LSTM  hardware  accelerator  can  achieve  a  throughput  of about 1.9 frames per second on a single video stream with a 1GHz 1024-bit processor, utilizing approximately 18mW of power. This research provides a cutting-edge solution for the practical application of LSTM networks in video recognition and other sequence analysis tasks. In addition to the novel FDHT-LSTM algorithm and customized hardware accelerator, a unique fault-tolerant technique called the Fault-Tolerant FDHT-LSTM (FT-FHDT-LSTM) is also introduced, enabling the accurate recognition of video clips in the presence of equipment malfunctions. However, NLP models are often hindered by a reliance on extensive data availability, hindering their application to resource-constrained settings and unique tasks necessitating large-scale labeling. As a means of enhancing NLP data efficiency, data augmentation techniques have been investigated in recent years. R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. Additionally, this knowledge enables the derivation of the density of prime factors of a given degree that split completely in the extension, as well as the determination of the density of such primes for various polynomial families. The density of primes satisfying specific conditions, such as those related to the norm of a prime or the structure of the prime in the extension, can also be established. A key component of our approach involves the prime specialization technique, which provides insight into the behavior of polynomials and their Galois groups across different algebraic closures. This understanding is then utilized to analyze the structure of the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. A deeper exploration of this concept leads to the identification of the Galois group's order, which is expressed in a more intricate form that reflects the composite nature of the symmetric group. This composite group arises from the combination of the symmetric group S_n, which arises from the simple polynomial x^n = a, for an irreducible polynomial with coefficients in the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) and a polynomial with a Galois group isomorphic to the direct product of the symmetric group S_nd for each of its n distinct roots. This connection holds true for any m-fold iteration of the composite polynomial. We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  By comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated that a significant nonradiative energy barrier has a height of approximately 0.24 electron volts.  Additionally, we observed a significant delay between heating the sample and measuring its properties, which we attribute to the presence of angle-pinned domains in the diamond lattice.  We tested this by incorporating a titanium dioxide layer above the nitrogen-vacancy center and found a notable decrease in this delay to several hours at 1000 Kelvin, which we link to a slower diamond lattice relaxation process.  We also explored the effects of temperature and vacuum conditions on nitrogen-vacancy centers and found that by switching between high and low magnetic field strengths, we could reduce the toxicity-induced shifts in ODMR resonances by approximately half.  Our research provides valuable insights into the behavior of nitrogen-vacancy centers under harsh environmental conditions and may contribute to the development of robust diamond-based spin optics technologies.

A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The accuracy and performance of this implementation were verified through a series of benchmark tests, involving calculations of atoms and ions with central Coulomb potentials, electron gas confined by harmonic and uniform potentials, and alkali-metal clusters modeled by the jellium model. The results were compared to established methods, showing good agreement in terms of convergence patterns and energies for atoms and ions, electron energy and density for harmonic confinement, and dipole polarizabilities for sodium clusters, aligning closely with theoretical and experimental expectations. The distinction between orderly and chaotic behavior within complex networks of interdependent oscillators corresponds to varying functional states found in numerous applications, including active brain states and stable electrical grids. Researchers have lately shown substantial interest in explosive synchronization phenomena which enable sudden shifts between these states due to their rapid and drastic nature. Although previous studies have highlighted key attributes of complex systems capable of explosive synchronization, these analyses were primarily undertaken on a case-by-case basis. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. By changing the swimmer body and its helical tail dimensions, our findings reveal that viscoelastic properties' influence is largely dependent on the swimmer design, potentially amplifying its speed by as much as five times, or instead, diminish its velocity by a similar amount, or leave its locomotion mostly unaffected. Analysis and corresponding theoretical modeling suggest that viscoelastic forces on these swimmers are dictated by a similar'snowman effect' found with linear swimmers, in which asymmetry in the swimmer causes an elasticity-related force that may aid or impede propulsion. Moreover, we observe two additional control mechanisms exerted by the swimmer's geometry on its motion: force distribution along the helical tail and the creation of a fluid cavity at the swimmer's head. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach as well as general statistical analysis, our results showed that "social" learning versions resulted in an ergodic Markov Chain, characterized by frequent occurrence of states leading to NE play in the stationary distribution. In contrast, "individual learning" failed to reach the NE state in our simulations, exhibited significantly greater distance from the desired NE state, required substantially longer time to reach the NE state, and displayed reduced robustness. Ultimately, our findings confirmed that the majority of games reached a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "social" learning algorithms. In contrast, only a minor subset of games reached the NE when players used the "individual learning" algorithms. Our results also showed that the main advantage of the "social" learning algorithms arose when players used the same algorithm, a situation that represents the most challenging condition for reaching a NE in asymmetric information games. However, we also found that both "social" learning algorithms could reach the NE in some cases of asymmetric play, although these cases were extremely rare. Our study provides the first rigorous analysis of learning behavior in games with asymmetric information using genetic algorithms and offers insights into the design of learning algorithms to replicate players' behavior in positive theory models. Furthermore, our findings may inform the application of genetic algorithms to study co-evolutionary processes in various fields. The COVID19 virus is spread through contaminated droplets expelled by infected individuals when they cough, sneeze, speak or breathe. Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the infection's spread. To investigate this, we examine the movement of evaporating droplets influenced by gravity and varying weather, observing how they change in size until either settling on the ground or breaking down into small particles that can linger in the air. Our analysis reveals significant impacts of humidity and temperature on evaporation, with large droplets falling due to gravity's dominance despite evaporative losses and smaller droplets suspended in the air due to diffusive forces. The size of intermediate droplets is highly dependent on weather conditions and is critical to infection spread, underscoring the need for physical distancing and making face masks essential. An additional analysis of global data reveals the frequent formation of infected droplet sizes of up to 500 micrometers, with falls occurring on average 100 to 1000 seconds after infection, although this time can be much shorter or much longer, depending on wind speed and air stability. Additionally, we explore the possibility that dry, warm air may increase the transmission of large infected droplets and highlight the importance of public health policies that account for weather conditions and environmental factors. Software used for these simulations is available for download at https://github.com/alexsafy/evaporating-sphere. The COVID19 virus's ability to spread through contaminated droplets that evaporate under changing environmental conditions must be understood by public health officials, policymakers, and the general public, with implications for infection transmission and the development of public health strategies, such as physical distancing and face mask use. The data and models presented here should be useful for updating SEIR models of COVID19 transmission, considering the effects of weather conditions and the resulting droplet sizes, and for addressing similar public health concerns, like the transmission of influenza and SARS viruses, with the appropriate adaptation of the model. The model's limitations highlight the difficulty in accurately predicting the spread of airborne viruses, emphasizing the need for further research into the physical and biological processes involved, with an emphasis on high-resolution data on droplet sizes, air stability, and wind speed. Ultimately, the implications of these findings for infection transmission and public health policies must be considered in the context of the underlying biology, data quality issues, and the limitations of the models used, with an acknowledgment of the need for further research into the spread of airborne viruses. Furthermore, the framework can be used to develop new methods for solving linear and nonlinear problems and can be used to incorporate physical constraints into scientific machine learning models. The framework introduced in this research can also be used to develop new methods for the uncertainty quantification of model errors and can be used to incorporate model errors into scientific machine learning models. Moreover, we have found that our generalized version can be represented in a supergravity-like form, and we have derived the specific conditions under which it becomes a 7-brane twist. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. The model's ability to learn from multiple languages was further verified by conducting a set of ablation experiments. The proposed method also facilitates cluster visualization, demonstrating its effectiveness through a case study on identifying linguistic traits. The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation errors that significantly impede the robust training of models. The recent releases of refined datasets, MultiWOZ 2.1 to 2.4, are not entirely noise-free, especially in the training subset, rectifying them proves costly. Instead of addressing the issues of annotation quality in the current datasets, we develop a versatile framework named ASSIST, aiming to train dialogue state tracking models with high reliability even from inaccurate labels. The proposed framework first uses an auxiliary model trained on a smaller clean dataset to generate accurate labels for each data sample, then utilizes both the generated pseudo labels and existing flawed labels for the training of the primary model. The framework is mathematically justified and is experimentally verified to boost the dialogue state tracking joint goal accuracy by up to 28.16% on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and 8.41% on the MultiWOZ 2.4 dataset compared to training from just flawed labels alone. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/tuoyou/ASSIST. The framework's effectiveness is further solidified by the observation that adding just one clean dataset with 500 training data samples is enough to enhance the model performance by 5.46%. The time-consuming and costly process of producing clean labels is thus avoided. The proposed framework may also be applied to other label-noise no noisrobust machine learning tasks. The statistics of label errors in dialogue state tracking are for the first time systematically studied, showing that the primary source of the annotation errors is the incorrect assignment of action types. In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. To address this, the model was modified to include an additional term representing individuals' willingness to participate in riots when they observe nearby unrest, along with a parallel model for accounting of population movement. The updated model significantly outperformed the original in predicting Santiago's rioting patterns. Furthermore, the model was validated using data from the city of Kinshasa, where the underlying dynamics differ substantially. Additionally, the project explores the conceptual similarities between this model and other approaches, such as the Merton model and epidemiological models incorporating behavioral changes, and finds that it is an uncommon case where a fractional Kirchhoff equation-based model is relevant to the study of social phenomena. The project's findings suggest that the Merton model may be applicable only in specific situations and that the previously reported results obtained with a particular scaling exponent may have been coincidental. The project also offers a potential explanation for the emergence of violent disturbances during the 2019 Chilean riots, along with implications for the model's applications to urban settings. The project's approaches to modeling complex social phenomena may also be of use to the broader scientific community. The project's findings and model developments may be relevant to research on the 2020 Nikolay Guryanov Bridge accident in Russia and the 2021 Tampa, Florida, pedestrian bridge accident in the United States. The project's techniques could be adapted to facilitate the detection of suspicious behavior indicators in biometrics-based surveillance systems. The project's most compelling advancement may be its demonstration of the utility of fractional differential equations in modeling the dissemination of new behaviors within a population. The project's most significant contribution is the development of a new approach to solving a fractional differential equation model, which may also be applied to the study of the dynamics underlying malicious propagation phenomena, such as the spread of malicious software, the propagation of malicious threats, and the dissemination of malicious propaganda. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. This method is applicable to any context-free language defined by a context-free grammar and is capable of handling a wide range of regular expressions, including those with intersection and complement operators. Furthermore, we demonstrate a symbolic approach to solving inequality problems with regular expressions, expressing the solution in terms of the original variables and character sets rather than normalized forms. This method also enables the derivation of contained relationships between regular expressions and context-free languages and can be executed with automaton-based decision procedures for determinism and containment. Additionally, we explore the applicability of this algorithm to the solution of systems of inequality problems with regular expressions and demonstrate its effectiveness through the solution of several complex containment problems with regular expressions, including some from renowned containment benchmark sets. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of relative containment and its association with safety properties in the context of programming languages, demonstrating the utility of this algorithm in determining whether a program contains another program and is thus safe. This research also introduces the design of a prototype implementation of this algorithm, demonstrating its efficiency and an instance of its application in the solution of containment problems in the context of string constraints. Additionally, we provide an outline for the extension of this algorithm to handle nested regular expressions and the design of a prototype implementation of this extension. Furthermore, we explore the generalization of this algorithm to determine whether one context-free language contains another and is thus equivalent, as well as the extension of this algorithm to handle nested regular expressions and context-free inequalities. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. This work is particularly relevant to the growing field of square-root topological quantum mechanics, enabling a deeper understanding of exotic phenomena arising from double-helix layer couplings in 3D solid-state systems. This discovery is further solidified by our demonstration of SHOWS states in double-helix layer couplings, which may provide a new path to realizing other complex topological states mediated by linear dispersion near Weyl point projections. Additionally, we propose modifying the double-helix layer couplings to create a SHOWS state with multiple Weyl points, which could serve as a key component for implementing quantum gates within a topological quantum computer. This implementation utilizes the unique hinge states connecting the projections of multiple Weyl points, which could serve as a showable, invisible path for a quantum processor error correction. This advancement offers a new way to construct topological quantum electrodynamics systems using layer couplings in 3D solid-state systems. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. Furthermore, FedSA excels particularly in scenarios where there is a significant difference between the data sets of the teacher and student, or when there are various classes within the teacher datasets. To facilitate collaborative FedSA research, we opened up a new dataset comprising 10 classes, categorized into three main areas, and made it available on both MNAR and MNIST frameworks. Our code has been freely shared on GitHub. With FedSA, we aim to create opportunities for researchers and practitioners to develop innovative methods that can efficiently combine knowledge from disparate sources. With the growth of cloud-based machine learning services, FedSA may eventually surpass centralized learning methods. Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, provided the $\alpha$-effect is localized to the tachocline. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. Additionally, we explore methods to enhance the visibility of local fluctuations in carrier concentration and dielectric properties using a vector calibration technique. The implementation of this method on the study of quantum processors will be discussed. Furthermore, we discuss the potential of utilizing mid-infrared spectroscopy to investigate the local phenomena and recommend studies on the carrier dynamics in silicon-based materials. Additionally, we discuss the potential of utilizing quantum interfaces based on magnetic moments to achieve near-field optical microscopy at the quantum level. variety, we develop the $\mathcal{A}$-twisted motivic spectral sequence.
By determining the motivic twisted algebraic $K$-theory spectrum as a twisted form
