The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Additionally, this report provides a valuable resource for teaching the relationship between thermodynamics and statistical mechanics. It demonstrates the precision of the thermodynamic limit and the consistency between thermodynamic and statistical mechanics calculations, serving as a valuable lesson for students. Furthermore, this report includes a discussion on the limitations and misconceptions regarding negative absolute temperature, along with an exploration of its practical applications. It is recommended that this topic be introduced through the simplest possible means, using a single-particle system, to avoid potential confusion. Moderately complex systems, such as a harmonic oscillator, are also explored in this report. It is the author's hope that this report will motivate others to share their own positive experiences with negative absolute temperature with the physics education community. Dually, the author is eager to learn from the experiences of others in teaching this subject. Any input or suggestions are welcome and will be incorporated into this report. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization. UniToPatho is unique in its comprehensive spectrum, covering normal and dysplastic areas, as well as polyps characterized as hyperplastic, serrated adenomas, and carcinomas. A novel numerical approach has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh adaptation technique which minimizes the required computational degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing performance by limiting support to the wave front's spatial extent. To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions for even better results. Successful applications and examples highlight the method's efficiency and adaptability with various sources, including external points and soft-scattering scenarios. However, it should be noted that trapping modes significantly reduce the method's efficiency. An optimization of the mesh is achieved using an adaptive finite element method based on an exponential stabilizer, resulting in more accurate results and confirming the method's efficiency for scattering problems. Furthermore, an analytical study on the Fourier transform of the time-domain solution is also presented, providing insight into the problem's behavior, especially in the high-frequency regime. A significant aspect of this study is the identification of the dominant term in the time-harmonic solution, allowing the development of an alternative method that bypasses the Fourier transform. This alternative approach involves a direct finite element time-harmonic solution, leveraging the mesh adaptation technique and resulting in enhanced performance. This includes the utilization of an explicit time-stepping method, and both direct and indirect approaches yield comparable results. Moreover, an explicit time-stepping method is introduced, and the paper is concluded by outlining the extension of this method to elastic scattering problems. This includes the formulation of the time-harmonic problem, the time-domain problem, and the adaptive finite element time-harmonic solution. Additionally, an explicit time-stepping method is proposed for this extended application. This method has a clear advantage of using an explicit scheme, and successfully addresses issues such as numerical dissipation, and source term, and also includes the utilization of an exponential stabilizer. We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating various processes on small parent bodies, our analysis suggested minimal water loss during thermal metamorphism, and the water content in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals can be explained by a mixture of D-poor nebular hydrogen and D-rich water from mesostases. Approximately 45-95$\%$ of water with low D isotope values in the pyroxene minerals came from nebular hydrogen, and it's possible that S-type asteroids with nominally anhydrous minerals can hold significant amounts of water (254-518 ppm). This finding may imply a reduced need for additional volatile delivery to the terrestrial planets during the final stages of planetary accretion, given the water added to the nominally dry inner Solar System bodies during the accretion process. However, the same research also suggests that some inner Solar System asteroids like Benenitra and Chelyabinsk chondrite parent bodies might have had enhanced water contents, potentially up to 130 ppm, although this would still be less than the water found in the water-rich CM chondrites. This amount of water could have been lost during the accretion of the terrestrial planets, explaining the distinct differences in the D isotope values seen in the bulk isotopic composition of the planets. Additionally, the water added to the planets from the partially dried inner Solar System asteroids could have been delivered in the form of hydrated minerals rather than pure water, leading to an incomplete equilibration of the D isotope values in the planets and providing a possible explanation for the observed variations in the D isotope values in the meteorites. This implies that the volatile delivery to the terrestrial planets should be further investigated by considering multiple sources of water, such as water contained within the hydrated minerals of the Small Parent Bodies, in addition to water released from the nebular hydrogen, and that the D isotope values in the planets could provide a means to differentiate between these various sources of water.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find exact expressions for scalar products and form factors of higher-spin XXZ chains. This applies to any spin values and mixtures thereof. We verify the affine quantum-group symmetry, $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$, for the XXZ chain's monodromy matrix, enabling exact derivation. Specifically, we use quantum-group symmetry to explicitly obtain diagonalized forms for the B and C operators within the F-basis of the spin-1/2 XXZ chain. This achievement substantiates prior conjectures about the algebraic Bethe-ansatz's correlation function calculations. These results provide a crucial foundation for systematic studies of form factors and correlation functions across solvable models connected to integrable XXZ spin chains. Additionally, we reveal the affine quantum-group symmetry's implications on spin chain's unitary representations and suggest a pattern that may unify various XXZ chain representations. Furthermore, we establish a relation between Bethe-ansatz equations and the quantum-group symmetry, resulting in a realization of the spin chain as a quasiparticle system conforming to the quantum group's symmetry. This profound understanding enables exploration of physical phenomena arising from the interplay between quasiparticles and the introduction of impurities into the spin chain. Lastly, we outline future directions for utilizing these findings in the study of physical systems. Experimental observation of quasiparticle behavior is suggested, along with the potential for impurity-induced phase transitions. Additionally, we highlight the importance of unitary matrix product states and quantum group symmetry in the study of interacting quantum many-body systems. Consequently, we expect the advancements made here to contribute significantly to the further exploration of physical systems made up of interacting quantum particles. Furthermore, our work is expected to lead to the development of more precise numerical approaches, specifically tailored at studying the physical properties of these systems across various regimes, as well as to the identification of new phases and phase transitions in quantum many-body systems. Additionally, our findings are anticipated to facilitate the development of novel applications for spin chains, such as their utilization in the study of biological processes, as well as the creation of new protocols for quantum information processing, such as quantum teleportation, superdense coding, and entanglement swaping, among others. Lastly, our research is expected to facilitate the development of custom-made unitary matrix product states, as well as the development of impurity-induced phase transitions, and we anticipate that these developments will, in turn, lead to the discovery of new phenomena in physics

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to the limited availability of multilingual models. We delve into zero-shot speech-to-text, which assumes no direct data or training is available for the target language. While similar challenges exist, we must also account for speech-specific difficulties. Existing methods primarily rely on combining speech recognition and machine translation models but are limited in scope. We, however, propose a novel zero-shot speech-to-text model that utilizes speech features and phonetic representations, bridging the gap between speech and text. Our approach is versatile, enabling easy extension to multilingual models. Notably, we explore phonetic-aware loss functions that facilitate better text-to-speech and speech-to-text performance. Our results indicate that our model excels over state-of-the-art baselines and is on par with multilingual models in terms of speech-to-text accuracy and phonetic accuracy. Moreover, we find that phonetic-aware loss functions are crucial for zero-shot speech-to-text. Our model and code have been made publicly available. High data-quality languages pose yet another challenge for low-quality target languages due to domain displacement. Our analysis reveals that phonetic confusion matrix is a reliable indicator of speech-to-text challenges. In response, we propose adjusting the data distribution to mitigate displacement effects. We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime. The accuracy of the calculated optical force is validated experimentally with observations of the radiation force-induced movement of an amorphous silicon sphere. Furthermore, we explore the distinction between optical force and torque and examine the impact of choice of material on the calculation of multipoles. The method is also applicable to systems comprising multiple particles. The utility of multipoles is also shown through the calculation of optical force in a dielectric sphere-double sphere configuration. The method is available as a software package called multipolarforce. The accuracy of the method is verified by comparison with experimental data on the motion of silicon spheres. The software can be accessed at https://github.com/alexsolano/multipolarforce. The optical force is shown to be sensitive to the choice of material, its dielectric function, and whether it is considered an electric or magnetic dipole. The method is an important development for the study of the interaction of light with matter at the microscale and can be combined with other methods such as the time-dependent density functional theory. The method can also be extended to consider not just the electric multipoles but also the magnetic multipoles. The method provides a detailed description of the interaction between light and matter at the microscale and can be used to study a wide range of phenomena resulting from the interaction between light and matter. The method can also be used to study the distribution of optical forces and the motion of particles composed of semiconductors, metals, and dielectrics. The method can be applied to any particle regardless of the accuracy of the dipolar approximation and can be used to study the scattering and optical force calculations beyond the long wavelength approximation. The method can be combined with experimental measurements such as the tracking of the motion of silicon spheres to verify the accuracy of the method. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. Moreover, we provide a public repository for our data, encompassing numerous 4d and 5d transition metal oxide combinations across various electron fillings, to facilitate the exploration of additional compounds. This research is also applicable to exploring the effects of electron-electron and electron-lattice interactions on transition metal oxides within other crystal structures. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Furthermore, our team created an interactive demonstration that was presented at the Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition 2021, allowing users to explore GAN-based medical imaging enhancement. Our research has since been made publicly available on the website https://disease-aware-edit.org/. In this report, we detail the underlying methodology used in our research and present the current capabilities and limitations of GAN-based medical imaging enhancement. Additionally, we outline potential directions for future development and utilization in the healthcare field. Our interactive demonstration was shortlisted for the Best Demo Award at the 2021 Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, smooth functions and a backward-stable solver for linear systems allow this approximation to be accurate over a grid cell when done correctly. In this paper, we provide a precise proof of this concept. We demonstrate our algorithm's effectiveness through several numerical experiments. In one scenario, we modify the boundary integral equation algorithm for finding the location of a disk within a plane by significantly reducing the computational time from exponential to linear with respect to the inverse of the radius by switching from a grid-based method to our new method. Furthermore, when the boundary consists of $N$ points, the time complexity becomes approximately $O(N)$. In another experiment, we solve a volume integral equation for a plane using our new method and compare the results with existing methods. In addition, we derive a new boundary condition algorithm that determines the height of one point based on the values of all other points along a line, leading to a significant reduction in computational time from $O(N^2)$ to $O(N)$.
